title: Does defective investigation necessarily produce false belief?
en:
**He says:** “As for defective investigation…”

Those who hold that sound investigation with its conditions entails knowledge disagree whether defective investigation entails ignorance, meaning noncorresponding belief. The Imām says it does: someone believing that the world is beginningless and that everything beginningless is independent of an agent cannot fail to believe that the world is independent of an agent.

Others say that it entails ignorance if the defect is confined to matter, but not otherwise. In the first case, a syllogism meeting the formal conditions necessarily entails its conclusion, whether its premises are true or false, as in the example. In the second, formal defect means precisely that the reasoning is not one of the moods entailing a conclusion.

The correct account is that neither kind necessarily entails ignorance. This is evident with defective form. Where only the matter is defective and the form is valid, a consequence of falsehood need not itself be false. Someone may believe that the world is the effect of an intrinsically necessitating agent and that every effect of an intrinsically necessitating agent is temporally originated. This entails that the world is temporally originated, which is true although both premises are false. Defective investigation can nevertheless yield ignorance, as in the preceding example concerning the beginningless world's independence.

More precisely, everyone agrees that formally defective reasoning does not entail [the conclusion], while reasoning defective only in matter sometimes entails ignorance and sometimes does not. The Imām intends a particular affirmative proposition, as his example shows; we deny the universal affirmative, because the entailment fails with some matter.

Those who deny entailment altogether mean an entailment grounded in a feature of the specious argument itself. Such an argument has no intrinsic feature or mode of indication grounding a necessary connection between it and the sought conclusion. Otherwise its indication would not disappear when its error became apparent; investigators, and even those protected from error, would be more likely to acquire ignorance by considering it, since they are better able to discern its mode of indication.

A genuine proof, by contrast, possesses an intrinsic feature and mode of indication grounding its entailment of the conclusion when the conditions are met. Entailment resulting instead from the investigator's belief in particular cases—for example, believing the premises of the example true—is undisputed.

The Imām objects that a truthful investigator's failure to acquire ignorance from an opponent's specious argument may result from failing to discern its aspect of entailment or failing to believe its premises, just as an opponent's considering a truthful person's proof does not necessarily yield knowledge. The claim that the truthful person is better able to discern the argument's force applies only to what yields truth and knowledge, not to what yields falsehood and ignorance.

title: Two conditions shared by sound and unsound inquiry
en: **He says: “Investigation Three: It is a condition…”** For inquiry (*naẓar*), whether sound or defective, two things are required in addition to the conditions of knowledge—life, intellect, absence of sleep and heedlessness, and the like. First, one must not already know the object sought (*maṭlūb*), since seeking has no place where attainment has already occurred. Second, one must not be in compound ignorance concerning it, that is, one must not decisively affirm its contradictory; such conviction prevents one from undertaking the search. On Abū Hāshim's view, this is because inquiry must be accompanied by doubt, whereas compound ignorance accompanies firm conviction, and the two conflict. On the philosophers' view, inquiry need not accompany doubt, but compound ignorance turns the person away from seeking, just as eating is discouraged by being full. The Qāḍī adopts the latter position; the Ustādh even holds that an investigator cannot be doubting.

title: General and special impediments: a criticism of al-Mawāqif
en:
Our brief presentation is clearer than that in *al-Mawāqif*: after life, the latter specifies reason and the absence of what opposes inquiry. Some impediments are general, opposing every apprehension as well as inquiry—sleep and heedlessness, for example. Others oppose inquiry specifically without opposing every apprehension: knowledge of the very conclusion being sought and compound ignorance concerning it.

One might object that compound ignorance already opposes knowledge; its absence is therefore included among knowledge's conditions, so to mention it here is redundant. The answer is that compound ignorance about *this conclusion* opposes knowledge *of this conclusion*, not knowledge without qualification. Its absence is therefore not simply one of the general conditions of knowledge. It is likewise unsatisfactory to interpret the general opponent in *al-Mawāqif* as that which opposes knowledge and every apprehension, and the special opponent as that which opposes knowledge alone, exemplified by already knowing the conclusion or being compoundly ignorant of it. [The digital text's final evaluative idiom, **كلام من قبيل الثاني**, needs independent confirmation; it is not used to invent a separate classification.]

title: Why further proofs can still be investigated
en:
If lack of knowledge of the conclusion is a condition of inquiry, one might object that after the first proof has established it one could never consider a second or third proof. The answer is that the condition holds where the aim of inquiry is to *obtain* knowledge or opinion. A person may nevertheless go through the procedure of investigation and inference for another purpose: to increase his own reassurance through mutually supporting proofs, or to assist a learner who becomes ready to accept several proofs together, or one particular proof rather than another. Minds differ in their receptivity to certainty. One person may be convinced by one proof, another by a different proof, and another by their combination, as happens with persuasive arguments.

The Imām says that considering a second proof means considering *the aspect in virtue of which it proves* the conclusion: what is still unknown is whether that argument proves it. This is a necessary concomitant, but it is not strictly the *maṭlūb* or *conclusion*: these terms name what follows intrinsically and determinately from the premises, the proposition whose subject is the minor premise's subject and whose predicate is the major premise's predicate.

title: Evidence, indicated conclusion, indication, and basis of indication
en:
Sound investigation further requires considering a genuine *dalīl*, not a specious argument (*shubha*), and considering it specifically in respect of its *dalāla*: that through which the mind passes from the evidence to what it indicates. Suppose we infer the Maker from the world by considering the world and obtaining two propositions: **the world has originated** and **every originated thing has a maker**, so that their arrangement teaches us that the world has a Maker.

For theologians the *world* is the evidence, unlike the logicians' usage in which the ordered pair of premises itself is the proof. The Maker's being established is what is indicated (*madlūl*). The world's being of such a kind that reflection upon it can yield knowledge that the Maker is established is its indication (*dalāla*). The world's possibility or origination—what makes it need an efficient cause—is the *aspect of indication* (*jihat al-dalāla*). These four are different in the sense that what each signifies conceptually is not what the others signify; accordingly, cognitions concerned with them differ in respect of their objects.

title: Is knowledge of a proof's evidential force knowledge of its conclusion?
en:
The Proof of Islam [al-Ghazālī] says that in a syllogism the aspect of indication is noticing that the conclusion is present potentially in the premise. This troubles weaker thinkers, who cannot determine whether the aspect of indication is identical with what is indicated. The truth is that the sought conclusion is the actually produced *madlūl*, and is other than noticing its potential presence in the premise.

In general, the familiar controversy here concerns whether the *aspect of indication* is other than the indicated conclusion, and from that follows the controversy over whether cognition of one is other than cognition of the other. Thus the Imām al-Rāzī and others report disagreement about whether knowledge of how the proof indicates differs from knowledge of the indicated proposition. The correct position is that they differ, because the indicated thing and the aspect of indication differ.

*Al-Mawāqif* instead reports the controversies as whether knowing the evidence's indication differs from knowing its conclusion, and whether the aspect of indication differs from the evidence itself. I have not found this framing in the well-known books, although the Imām, when explaining the distinction between knowing the aspect of indication and knowing the indicated conclusion, mentions three things: knowing the evidence itself, such as knowing the world's possibility; knowing the indicated thing itself, such as knowing that it must have a cause; and knowing that the evidence is evidence for what is indicated. The first two plainly differ, and the third differs from both, since it is knowledge of a relation (*iḍāfa*) between evidence and indicated thing, other than either. This might suggest a controversy about the distinctness of knowledge of the *dalāla* from knowledge of the *madlūl*, because the distinction requires explicit demonstration. Using the world's possibility—although it is the *aspect* of indication—as an example of knowing the evidence itself might likewise suggest that the aspect of indication is the evidence itself.

title: Al-Rāzī's Naqd al-Muḥaṣṣal and the status of a relation
en:
In *Naqd al-Muḥaṣṣal* there is language suggesting dispute over whether the aspect of indication must differ from both the evidence and the thing indicated. It says that theologians debate this while arguing from the existence of everything other than God to God's existence. They contend that the aspect in virtue of which the existence of other things indicates God's existence cannot be distinct from both: whatever differs from God's existence belongs to the existence of what is other than God, whereas what differs from the existence of everything other than God is God's existence alone.

The answer offered there is that knowledge of the aspect of the evidence's indicating its object—supposedly distinct from both—is an intellectual consideration (*amr iʿtibārī ʿaqlī*), not something existing externally. But, as you know, it is the *evidence's indication of the object* that is a relational, conceptually posited matter; that is not the *aspect of indication*, which is a property of the evidence, such as possibility or origination in the world. Moreover, the wording apparently makes the subject said to be conceptually posited *knowledge of the aspect of indication*. Its error is evident. [This translation preserves the author's criticism, rather than attributing the whole treatment indiscriminately to al-Rāzī.]

title: Is a teacher indispensable for knowledge of God?
en:
**On his words: “A teacher's existence is not a condition for inquiry into knowledge of God Most High.”** This is against the position of the group the text calls *al-malāḥida*. We have several arguments. First, we have established that sound inquiry meeting its conditions produces knowledge without qualification: in divine matters as in others, and whether accompanied by a teacher or not. The possibility of gathering immediate premises and arranging them productively with the aid of logic is itself evident.

Second, the teacher's own inquiry into knowledge of God would require yet another teacher, and so on without end—unless the demand for instruction is restricted to people other than the teacher himself and the teacher's inquiry is declared sufficient because he receives special divine support; or the sequence of instruction is brought to an end at a teacher whose knowledge rests upon the Prophet, peace be upon him, and ultimately upon revelation.

title: The regress involved in certifying the teacher
en: Third, a teacher's guidance benefits us only once we know that he is truthful. Either we know his truthfulness through investigation—in which case investigation is enough to reach knowledge, since it establishes the truthfulness of the teacher through whom knowledge is supposedly obtained—or through that teacher's own statement. The second alternative is circular: his assertion that he speaks truth cannot prove that he does so unless we already know him to be truthful. Or we know it through the statement of another teacher, and thus continue without end.

title: A reply made on behalf of instruction
en: An answer may be offered: we do not hold that the teacher independently produces knowledge, so we do not require prior knowledge that he is invariably truthful. Rather, productive inquiry is inquiry accompanied by his guidance to the proofs and his removal of doubts and specious objections. Our intellects are too limited to infer correctly without this assistance and need an imam who teaches evidence and how to answer difficulties. Through his teaching together with the power of our own intellects, we obtain knowledge of divine realities, including that he is an imam entitled to guide and instruct.

title: Distinguishing the attainment of knowledge from salvation
en:
Notice, however, that even if the foregoing arguments are sound, they deny only the need for a teacher *in obtaining knowledge*. Suppose instead the opponents mean that one needs him for *salvation*: that someone's knowledge achieved by inference does not save him unless instruction is connected to it, received from a teacher, and accepted in obedience to his command. The text adduces the prophetic statement about being commanded to fight until people profess that there is no god but God, and the revealed commands “Know that there is no god but God” and “Say: He is God, One.” Many people who acknowledged a Maker and His oneness were nonetheless unbelievers because they did not receive this from the Prophet, peace be upon him, or comply with his command.

The proper reply in that case is: what your position amounts to is a need, for salvation, for a teacher whose veracity is established by miracles. That teacher is the Prophet, peace be upon him, and he suffices as imam and guide until the Resurrection. There is no need in each age for another teacher to renew the institution of guidance, with salvation made dependent on following him and acknowledging his imamate. The opponents' argument and the reply to it are clear from the concise text. [The argument about salvation is reported as part of a historical debate; the sectarian designation is the source's, not an editorial judgment.]

title: The obligation of investigation: its fundamental argument
en:
**He says: “Investigation Four: There is no disagreement among the people of Islam concerning the obligation of inquiry for knowledge of God Most High.”** This means inquiry for the purpose of obtaining that knowledge to the extent human capacity permits. The inquiry is within our power, and an unconditional obligation (*wājib muṭlaq*), namely knowledge, depends upon it. Whatever is within one's power and upon which an unconditional obligation depends is itself obligatory: by revelation if the primary obligation derives from revelation, as we hold; or by reason if it derives from reason, as the Muʿtazila hold. Otherwise the imposition of an impossible task would follow.

That inquiry is within one's power is evident. Knowledge depends upon it because such knowledge is not immediate but inferential; “inferential” means precisely what depends upon and is obtained by inquiry. As for the obligation of knowledge, among us it is grounded in revelation, the texts concerning it, the consensus established upon it, and the dependence of all other obligations upon it.

title: The Muʿtazilī argument from avoiding anticipated harm
en:
According to the Muʿtazila, knowledge is obligatory by reason because it averts anticipated harm: fear of punishment in the hereafter when numerous people have reported it, and fear of the worldly harms produced by sectarian disagreements about knowing the Maker—wars, loss of life, and destruction of property. Reason requires preventing even doubtful, not merely probable, harm: if someone is about to take a road and is warned that an enemy or predatory beast lies along it, he should take precautions.

The reply denies that fear is generally probable. Most people need not be aware of such disagreement, its destructive consequences, the Maker, or reports of afterlife reward and punishment; only some people receive those reports. And even where they do, truth is not more probable than falsehood on the premises of this inquiry, since knowledge of the Maker, the prophets' missions, and the evidential force of miracles has not yet been established. Even granting anticipated fear, we deny that acquiring the alleged knowledge removes it: the possibility of error remains, along with fear of punishment or discord, while the exertion is an additional burden.

One might say that the knowledgeable person is plainly in a better state than the ignorant, possessing a perfection that reason requires us to acquire. We reply: yes, **if** the knowledge is properly obtained; but that is not certain, and an inquirer may instead fall into the valleys of error and be destroyed. Hence the saying that simplicity may be closer to safety than truncated cleverness. This is all after conceding the duty to seek the better state. Our formulation completes the earlier argument by establishing the obligation of knowledge; *al-Mawāqif* instead treats the inquirer's being in a better state as a direct argument for the rational obligation of inquiry.

en: Several difficulties have been raised against this argument. Some are not peculiar to it and need not be resolved here: they merely challenge premises that have already been established, such as inquiry's producing knowledge in general or in divine matters, its doing so without a teacher, the possibility of establishing and transmitting consensus, and consensus's probative authority. Five difficulties are more specific to this argument and require an answer.

title: First objection: can an already knowledgeable or inattentive person be commanded to know?
en:
**First:** The obligation of knowledge presupposes the possibility of making it obligatory. But to impose it upon someone who already knows would command the acquisition of what is already acquired—impossible. To impose it on someone who does not know would command the inattentive person (*ghāfil*), which is invalid.

The answer is that such an obligation is evidently possible. The premise about inattention fails: an inattentive person in this sense is one to whom the address has not reached, or has reached but is not understood; it does not mean anyone who lacks knowledge of the matter commanded. Thus one commanded to know that the world has a beginningless Maker characterized by knowledge and power may already understand the concepts expressed by these words, while being commanded to attain assent to that proposition and to conceive those concepts to the extent of human capacity.

To impose it on someone who does not know would command the inattentive person (ghāfil), which is invalid.

The answer is that such an obligation is evidently possible. The premise about inattention fails: an inattentive person in this sense is one to whom the address has not reached, or has reached but is not understood; it does not mean anyone who lacks knowledge of the matter commanded. Thus one commanded to know that the world has a beginningless Maker characterized by knowledge and power may already understand the concepts expressed by these words, while being commanded to attain assent to that proposition and to conceive those concepts to the extent of human capacity.

title: Second objection: scripture, consensus and imitation
en:
**Second:** We do not concede that there is evidence making knowledge obligatory. The scriptural text, for example “Know that there is no god but God,” does not signify obligation with certainty, since a command may have another force. Consensus is not transmitted with certainty, because it has supposedly been reported only by isolated transmissions rather than through tawātur. The opponent may deny it and even claim consensus that assent suffices, whether it is knowledge, opinion, or imitation (*taqlīd*). The Companions and Followers accepted ordinary people's imitation and submission without obliging them to perform technical investigation and demonstration.

The reply is that probability is sufficient for establishing a legal obligation. Moreover, the consensus concerned has been transmitted so widely that collusion on falsehood is impossible, and therefore yields certainty. The alleged consensus on sufficient imitation is misconceived: the early community accepted the knowledge derived from **general or summary proofs** (*adilla ijmāliyya*), as in the Qurʾānic question, “If you ask them who created the heavens and earth, they will surely say: God.” They did not require people to formulate premises in exact syllogistic order, determine conditions of valid production, set out every issue with its proofs, and present objections together with their answers. Even if it were established that mere imitation suffices for certain people, that would not negate the obligation of knowledge through inquiry and inference in general.

title: Individual and collective obligations of proof
en: The truth is that **knowledge by a summary proof, which raises its investigator out of the low condition of mere imitation, is an individual obligation (*farḍ ʿayn*) from which no legally responsible person is exempt**. [This is al-Taftāzānī's explicit normative conclusion, not a claim that every layperson must master the terminology or forms of scholastic logic.]

title: Third objection: instruction, inspiration, an infallible imam and spiritual purification
en:
**Third:** We deny that complete knowledge can only be obtained through inquiry. It might be obtained through teaching, as the *malāḥida* maintain; through inspiration, as the Brahmins maintain; through an infallible imam's word, as the Shīʿa maintain; or through purification of the inward self by spiritual exercises and struggle, as the Sufis maintain.

We answer that it is evident that the acquisition of non-immediate cognitions requires **some** inquiry, outward or concealed. This is clear with teaching, which consists in helping reason by pointing to premises and eliminating doubts and specious arguments. Some compare the inward eye's inquiry with the outward eye's seeing, and the teacher's words with physical light: just as sight needs the eye and light, knowledge needs inquiry and instruction. The same is true of an infallible imam: another purportedly infallible person's assurance of his truthfulness is insufficient unless, ultimately, one reaches rational inquiry. Inspiration inspires confidence only if its recipient knows it is from God, and this requires inquiry even if the recipient cannot put that inquiry into words. Inward purification counts as a source of religious knowledge only after the soul has attained reassurance regarding the truth, which likewise requires inquiry.

Moreover, even if some knowledge could be attained without inquiry, our position would not be harmed: we claim its necessity for the overwhelming majority. That does not exclude exceptional cases, for inquiry is manifestly the ordinary person's way.

title: Fourth objection: unconditional and conditional obligations
en:
**Fourth:** We deny that knowledge is an unconditional obligation. Such an obligation supposedly obtains under every circumstance, whereas the duty of knowledge is restricted to a state of doubt—that is, hesitation over the predicative relation—or at least to the absence of knowledge; someone already possessing it cannot be commanded to acquire it again.

The answer is that “unconditional” does not mean “obligatory in every conceivable circumstance.” Otherwise there would be no unconditional obligation, since a duty no longer demands performance once it has been performed. Fasting, for instance, is unconditional with respect to intention, which therefore has to be supplied, but conditional with respect to the person's being resident rather than travelling: the duty does not require one to establish residence. The pilgrimage is conditional on capacity, which need not be acquired, but unconditional with respect to entering consecration and similar means, which must be undertaken.

Rather, an obligation is unconditional relative to a prerequisite when it remains obligatory whether that prerequisite is present or absent. Knowledge is not conditional upon inquiry in the sense that one is required to know only *if one has already investigated*; otherwise it would not be unconditional in this respect. It **is**, however, conditional relative to doubt or absence of knowledge, since the already knowledgeable person is not obliged to know what he knows. Therefore acquiring doubt or nonknowledge is not obligatory. This also resolves a further objection based upon these conditions, omitted from the concise text because the disputes about whether they are within one's power and whether doubt is obligatory arise below.

title: Fifth objection: does the obligation of an end imply a command to its means?
en: **Fifth:** We deny that a prerequisite to an unconditional obligation must itself be obligatory. Someone could command a thing while overlooking its prerequisite, or even expressly declaring that prerequisite not obligatory. If one objects that requiring an end without its prerequisite imposes an impossibility, we reply: what is impossible is the **existence** of the end without the **existence** of its prerequisite, not the **obligation** of the end without an **obligation** of the prerequisite. No impossibility arises from the latter. If one further argues that permitting omission of the prerequisite while still imposing the end amounts to commanding the impossible, we answer that something may be impermissible to omit because it is indispensable to a legally required act, and thus “obligatory” in the sense of **necessary**, without itself being a distinct object of the Legislator's commanding address. This latter, stricter sense is what is at issue.

title: The narrower reply: knowledge as a quality and inquiry as its attainable cause
en:
The answer is to restrict the claim. When what is commanded cannot be directly produced by a human being, whose power extends only to undertaking its causes, commanding the outcome is plainly commanding the undertaking of those causes. For example, a command to bring about an act necessarily concerns the execution of the instrumental acts through which it is brought about. Here knowledge itself is not an act directly within one's power but a *quality* (*kayfiyya*); commanding it can only mean commanding its cause, which is inquiry. This does not presuppose that imposing impossible tasks is intrinsically impossible, which would be an objection against our own position.

Since what is intended is the *revealed* obligation of inquiry, and consensus upon it has in fact been affirmed, there is no need for all these premises and answers. Even to show obligation merely without a conclusive proof, the outward sense of the Qurʾānic injunctions would suffice, such as “Look at the traces of God's mercy” and “Say: Look at what is in the heavens,” among others.

title: The Muʿtazilī challenge: would prophets be unable to require examination of their miracles?
en:
**He says: “They said that if it were obligatory only by revelation…”** The Muʿtazila argue that inquiry into a miracle, knowledge, and everything that establishes the revealed law must be obligatory by reason. Otherwise prophets would be *rendered unable to compel an answer* (*ifḥām al-anbiyāʾ*); their missions would have no benefit, an evidently unacceptable result.
The argument runs as follows. When a prophet tells someone, “Consider my miracle, so that my claim's truthfulness will become clear to you,” that person may respond: “I shall not investigate unless it is obligatory, since I may omit what is not obligatory. It cannot be obligatory for me before revelation is established, because no obligation exists except through revelation. But revelation cannot be established for me until I investigate, since its establishment is inferential rather than immediate.” If one objects that examining a miracle does not depend upon *being obligated* to examine it, the answer is that the prophet would nevertheless have no binding claim to demand inquiry, since what is not obligatory cannot be enforced. That is the sense of *ifḥām* here.

title: First answer: the objection also threatens rational obligation
en: The first reply is an argument *ad hominem* (*ilzām mushtarak*): a counterexample showing that the opponent's general argument undermines a position he himself accepts. If the opponent calls such rational obligation an obvious inferential truth, recognizable with the slightest attention or by hearing the Legislator state its premises, one may reply that the addressee can refuse even that attention or listening. The same *ifḥām* results.

title: Second answer: actual obligation is distinct from knowing its obligatoriness
en:
The second answer identifies the equivocation. A prophet's ability legitimately to require inquiry depends on the **actual existence** of inquiry's obligation and on the actual establishment of revelation, not on the addressee's knowing that either is the case. What depends on investigation is the person's *knowledge* of their establishment, not their establishment in reality.

If the objection refers throughout to the obligation and revelation themselves, then “revelation does not obtain unless I investigate” is false. If it refers throughout to knowledge of them, then “I need not investigate unless it is obligatory” is improperly stated: lack of knowledge of a duty does not itself negate its existence. If “I am not obliged” means actual obligation while “until revelation is established” means knowledge that revelation is established, the claim that one is not obliged before its establishment is false: being obliged does not depend on knowing one is obliged, whereas knowing an obligation depends on there being one, lest the knowledge be erroneous.

This is the import of *al-Mawāqif*'s wording: when it says that the addressee's assertion would hold only if actual obligation depended on knowledge of the obligation, the subsequent “we say…” supplies the predicate to that earlier construction, and the demonstrative points back to the assertion. Finally, if “revelation cannot be established until I investigate” refers to *knowledge*, but “I shall not investigate unless I am obliged” refers to *actual obligation*, the individual propositions may all be true, yet the argument's form fails because the middle term is not repeated with one meaning. It is a syllogism whose premises may be materially sound but whose form is invalid—unlike the other construal, which can have correct form but unsound premises.

title: Investigation Five: what is the first obligation?
en:
**Investigation Five:** They differ about the first thing obligatory upon a legally responsible person (*mukallaf*). The Shaykh says it is knowledge of God Most High, since that is the foundation of the other obligations. The Ustādh says it is inquiry into knowledge of God, as it is the prerequisite previously established. The Qāḍī and the Imām say it is the *intention to inquire*, upon which inquiry depends.

The truth is that if “first obligation” means the first thing intended for its own sake, it is knowledge; if it means the first obligation without that restriction, it is the intention to inquire. The latter position, however, rests on the obligation of a prerequisite to an unconditional obligation, with the difficulties already discussed. Thus the concise text says: “Otherwise, the second”—that is, inquiry or intending to inquire.

Someone might object that inquiry is conditioned on not knowing the conclusion, that is, simple ignorance of the object sought, so this should be first among the obligations. We answer that such ignorance is not itself within power, but precedes the exercise of power and will. Even if it were within power, inquiry's obligation is conditional upon it, because seeking what has already been attained is impossible; it is consequently not a prerequisite to an *unconditional* obligation. Maintaining ignorance, though something one can bring about by refraining from the causes of knowledge, is not itself a prerequisite to the obligation.

title: Abū Hāshim: must doubt come before inquiry?
en:
Abū Hāshim holds that the first obligation is doubt, because intending to inquire depends upon it: one must apprehend both terms and their relation without yet believing either the sought proposition or its contradictory, as explained earlier. Two replies have been made.

First, doubt is not directly within human power, because like knowledge it is a quality; what is within power is acquiring it or maintaining it, for example by conceiving the two terms and refraining from deciding their relation. Neither action, it is argued, is a prerequisite. *Al-Mawāqif* objects that if doubt were not within power, knowledge would not be either, since knowledge is its opposite and power is equally related to opposites. This falls by its own admission that knowledge as such is not directly within power, although obtaining knowledge by undertaking its causes is.

Second, the obligation of inquiry and knowledge is conditional upon doubt, since inquiry supposedly cannot occur without it, let alone be required. Doubt would therefore be a condition upon which the duty depends, rather than a means to an unconditional duty, like the taxable minimum (*niṣāb*) for alms or capacity for pilgrimage; there is no duty to bring it about. Since commanding knowledge amounts to commanding inquiry, *al-Mawāqif* accordingly says that knowledge's obligation is conditional upon doubt. Strictly, however, arguing that doubt is obligatory relies on its being a prerequisite of **inquiry**, not of knowledge.

title: Taftāzānī's reassessment of the objections to obligatory doubt
en:
Both objections are weak. Against the first: “within power,” as applied to a prerequisite, does not mean that the prerequisite must itself be a freely chosen act, but that the responsible person can *bring it about*, as one may acquire ritual purity for prayer or ownership of the taxable minimum for alms. Its being obligatory means that one must bring it about. Against the second: it would follow that inquiry and knowledge need not be obtained by someone who holds a weak contrary suspicion (*wahm*), a preponderant opinion (*ẓann*), an imitative belief (*taqlīd*), or compound ignorance. That consequence is plainly unsound.

One can reply concerning suspicion and opinion that “doubt” may encompass both, since it means indecision about a relation, whether the two possibilities are equal—as in doubt strictly so called—or one is more likely than the other, as with opinion and its weaker counterpart. As for imitation and compound ignorance, what is obligatory even in these states is considering the evidence and knowing its aspect of indication, so that these states may be transformed into knowledge. No one disputes that someone firmly convinced of the conclusion or of its contradictory does not, in that condition, actually undertake the *search* in the ordinary sense.

It may be added against strictly equal doubt that, even if it is a prerequisite for obligatory inquiry, it is not one of the *causes* whose obligation follows from commanding inquiry: it does not itself fall under a separate legal address. This reply calls for examination, since Abū Hāshim means rational obligation, like his account of inquiry and knowledge. A more appropriate objection would challenge whether doubt is among the things a rational agent positively seeks and for omitting which he judges blame deserved. title: Investigation Six: definition by essential and accidental characteristics
en:
**Investigation Six.** We have already indicated that the first motion in inquiry obtains the *matter* of a compound cognition capable of leading to the sought object, while the second obtains its *form*. What is sought is either conception (*taṣawwur*) or assent (*taṣdīq*). What leads to conception is called a *definer* (*muʿarrif*), either a definition by essential constituents (*ḥadd*) or a description (*rasm*), each complete or incomplete.

A defining expression must distinguish its object, since intellectual knowledge without distinction is impossible. If the distinguishing feature is intrinsic to the quiddity, the expression is called a *ḥadd*: literally a boundary or prohibition, as a definition must exclude what is outside the defined thing and not exclude what belongs to it. The expression that does so by essence and reality deserves this designation particularly. If the distinguishing feature is accidental to the quiddity, it is called *rasm*, like a trace by which one discovers a path.

If the distinguishing feature is accompanied by the complete common essential constituent—that which answers “What is it?” both for the quiddity and for everything sharing that constituent, the *proximate genus*—the definition is complete. A complete *ḥadd* includes all the essentials; a complete *rasm* includes the full common essential and the complete distinguishing accidental feature. Otherwise each is incomplete. Only one complete essential definition is possible: proximate genus together with proximate differentia, with the genus placed first. Reversing the order makes the definition incomplete.

This assumes that a common accident is not taken into account, since it neither distinguishes nor discloses the quiddity's parts, and that a peculiar property (*khāṣṣa*) added to the proximate differentia is not counted either. Otherwise a combination of proximate differentia with common accident or peculiar property would incorrectly count as an incomplete *ḥadd*, whereas in the dominant terminology a *ḥadd* consists purely of essentials. Some, by contrast, call every defining expression a *ḥadd*, including a merely verbal explanation: explaining what one expression means by another whose signification is clearer. Many earlier writers held that a complete *rasm* distinguishes the quiddity from **everything** other than it, and an incomplete one from only **some** things. Investigation Six. We have already indicated that the first motion in inquiry obtains the matter of a compound cognition capable of leading to the sought object, while the second obtains its form. What is sought is either conception (taṣawwur) or assent (taṣdīq). What leads to conception is called a definer (muʿarrif), either a definition by essential constituents (ḥadd) or a description (rasm), each complete or incomplete.

A defining expression must distinguish its object, since intellectual knowledge without distinction is impossible. If the distinguishing feature is intrinsic to the quiddity, the expression is called a ḥadd: literally a boundary or prohibition, as a definition must exclude what is outside the defined thing and not exclude what belongs to it. The expression that does so by essence and reality deserves this designation particularly. If the distinguishing feature is accidental to the quiddity, it is called rasm, like a trace by which one discovers a path.

If the distinguishing feature is accompanied by the complete common essential constituent—that which answers “What is it?” both for the quiddity and for everything sharing that constituent, the proximate genus—the definition is complete. A complete ḥadd includes all the essentials; a complete rasm includes the full common essential and the complete distinguishing accidental feature. Otherwise each is incomplete. Only one complete essential definition is possible: proximate genus together with proximate differentia, with the genus placed first. Reversing the order makes the definition incomplete.

This assumes that a common accident is not taken into account, since it neither distinguishes nor discloses the quiddity's parts, and that a peculiar property (khāṣṣa) added to the proximate differentia is not counted either. Otherwise a combination of proximate differentia with common accident or peculiar property would incorrectly count as an incomplete ḥadd, whereas in the dominant terminology a ḥadd consists purely of essentials. title: Three ways of reaching assent: syllogism, induction and analogy
en: What leads to assent is called *evidence* (*dalīl*) because it guides to the sought judgement, and an *argument* (*ḥujja*) because one gains the upper hand over an opponent by employing it. It is either syllogism (*qiyās*), induction (*istiqrāʾ*), or analogy (*tamthīl*). The argument must have an intelligible connection with what it seeks to establish. Either one contains the other or neither does. When the argument contains the sought conclusion, it is syllogism, because the conclusion is included within its premises. When the sought judgement encompasses the argument, it is induction: a universal judgement is established through its occurrence in the particular cases falling under it. When neither contains the other, a third factor must encompass or be shared by them so that knowledge of one can give knowledge of the other. This is analogy: the judgement concerning the new case (*farʿ*) is derived from the judgement concerning the original case (*aṣl*), both coming under the common factor, which is the cause (*ʿilla*).

title: Al-Rāzī and the problem of the “relative particular”
en:
Thus the Imām says: when we infer one thing from another, if neither falls under the other the procedure is analogy. If one falls under the other, inference from the universal to the particular is syllogism, and the reverse is induction. In some books he substitutes the *more general* and *more specific*, making clear that “particular” means **relatively particular**, not a particular in the strict sense. This also indicates that defining a relative particular as something included beneath another is equivalent to defining it as more specific than a more general item—not broader than that, as some have mistakenly thought. “Inclusion beneath” means that the other encompasses it **and something besides it**, not merely that the broader predicate happens to be true of it. Scholars do not ordinarily treat each of two coextensive concepts as relatively particular to the other.

Hence the author of *al-Ṭawāliʿ* says that syllogism includes inference from a universal to a particular *or from one of two coextensive terms to the other*. This includes an inference whose middle term is coextensive with the minor, such as “Every human is rational; every rational being is an animal.” To reply that “rational” means “a thing possessing rationality,” and is therefore broader than “human,” does not solve the problem: it cannot be used for “Every rational being is human; every human is an animal.”

A better answer is that syllogism derives a judgement about the subject falling under the minor term by considering the middle term's concept, which is certainly more general in that relevant application—even if the minor concept is coextensive with it, as in the two examples, or is in some respect broader. Thus one may reason: “Some animals are human; every human is rational”; “Some animals are human; no horse is human”; or “Every human is an animal; every human is rational.” A similar account applies to conjunctive conditional syllogisms, where universally stated positions or suppositions permit an inference in a particular instance. For exception-based syllogisms the point is less obvious unless they are reformulated in the first figure: “The consequent's content is such that its sufficient antecedent obtains; whatever has its sufficient antecedent obtains,” or “The antecedent's content is such that its necessary consequent is absent; whatever lacks a necessary consequent is absent.” Jurists use *qiyās* for analogy because it equates two particulars in a ruling by their equality in the cause. According to logicians, the parallel explanation for *qiyās* is that the unknown conclusion is put on the same footing as the premises in becoming known.

title: Conjunctive and exception-based syllogisms
en: If a syllogism includes its conclusion or the contradictory of that conclusion **explicitly**, in matter and form, even where a conditional particle prevents its clause from standing as a complete assertoric proposition, it is called an *exception-based syllogism* (*qiyās istithnāʾī*). Certain Arabic grammarians say that a statement can cease to be a complete assertion capable of truth and falsehood through an addition, as with a clause of a conditional, just as it can through an omission—for example in a defective formulation of “Zayd is learned” lacking what is required to complete its construction. The name “exception-based” refers to the affirmation or denial of one side of the conditional. Otherwise it is a *conjunctive syllogism* (*iqtirānī*) because its terms—minor, major, and middle—are joined to one another. The exception-based syllogism is **connected** if its conditional is connected and **disjunctive** if the conditional is disjunctive; the conjunctive syllogism is **categorical** if made wholly of categorical propositions and **conditional** if it includes a conditional proposition.

title: Complete and incomplete induction; certain and probable analogy
en:
Induction means surveying the particular instances of one universal to establish their judgement universally. It is *complete* when their enumeration is known to be exhaustive and the ruling is known for every one: this is a kind of conditional conjunctive syllogism called the *divisional syllogism* (*al-qiyās al-muqassam*). Otherwise it is incomplete, as the unqualified term usually indicates, and yields only opinion.

Analogy means showing that a particular agrees with another particular in the cause of its ruling so that they may be judged alike. It yields certainty if the shared factor is known independently to be the sufficient cause; in that event it is a form of syllogism and the illustrative original case is redundant. Otherwise it is probable, and this is what the unqualified term usually means. The detailed treatment of all these topics belongs to the discipline of logic.

title: Syllogistic forms in al-Ṭawāliʿ, the Imām and al-Mawāqif
en:
The author of *al-Ṭawāliʿ* gives, very elegantly and briefly, the productive moods of connected and disjunctive exception-based syllogisms and of all four figures of the categorical conjunctive syllogism. The Imām presents them more generally but omits the fourth figure as unnatural. He characterizes the third figure as two attributes occurring in one subject—that is, affirmation or negation of two things of a third. This includes syllogisms with a negative major premise, such as “Every human is an animal; no human is a neighing creature.” Humanity thus has animality affirmed of it and neighing denied of it, from which it is known that some animals are not neighing creatures.

He describes the disjunctive exception-based syllogism in terms of two exhaustive alternatives: deny either and establish the other, or affirm either and exclude the other. Because this wording appears limited to *exclusive and exhaustive* disjunction, the author of *al-Mawāqif* replaces it with a shorter, more general account: establish incompatibility between two propositions, so that establishing one entails excluding the other. In full detail, if they are incompatible in both truth and falsehood, the truth of either excludes the other's truth and the falsity of either excludes the other's falsity. If incompatible only in truth, affirming one excludes the truth of the other. If incompatible only in falsehood, the falsity of one excludes the falsity of the other.

title: What “evidence” means; how knowing evidence entails knowing what it indicates
en:
**He says: “And the term evidence may be used…”** In logic, *dalīl* names the ordered premises producing the conclusion. But it may also mean something one can examine and from which those ordered premises can be derived, such as the world in an argument for its Maker. In this second sense it is “that by sound inquiry into which one can attain a judgement,” whether certain or probable. “Can” is included because a proof does not lose its status as proof when no one happens to examine it; “sound” is specified because defective inquiry, including inquiry not directed to its evidential aspect, does not yield the judgement. “Judgement” is unrestricted so as to include what may be called an *indication* or *sign* (*amāra*). Many writers reserve *dalīl* for evidence yielding knowledge and *amāra* for that yielding opinion. *Istidlāl* is the process of reaching the judgement. It is sometimes reserved for proceeding from an effect to its cause, such as inferring the Maker from the world; the reverse direction is called *taʿlīl*, as when reasoning from fire to illumination—that is, to assent that illumination will occur.

When they say that a *dalīl* is what, when known, entails knowing the existence of the *madlūl*, the intended knowledge is knowledge of the realization of a relation, affirmative or negative. They are not restricting the conclusion to a positively existing thing merely because the word “indicated” is used: the account must allow inference from the absence of life to the absence of knowledge. Nor does the reciprocity of the terms *dalīl* and *madlūl* create a circle. In this usage, *dalīl* yields **assent**, not conception, while **knowledge** is one kind of assent contrasted with opinion.

Accordingly, if “knowing the evidence” refers to the world as evidence for the Maker, it means knowing the ordered premises derived by examining its evidential aspect **together with all the other conditions**, among them noticing how the syllogism produces its conclusion and how one content is included under another. Only then does knowing the evidence entail knowing the indicated conclusion. One might say: knowledge of the conclusion is a necessary concomitant of knowing ordered premises, but a non-obvious one whose recognition requires a middle term. We reply: if that were so, the first cognition could not occur without the second, any more than a triangle could exist without its angles being equal to two right angles. What requires a middle term is rather **knowing that the entailment holds**. A necessary concomitant cannot be separated from what entails it, whether obvious or non-obvious; the difference concerns knowledge of the necessity and of the concomitant's actual realization.

title: Rational, transmitted, and mixed proofs
en:
**He says: “And evidence…”** Evidence is sometimes divided into rational (*ʿaqlī*) and transmitted (*naqlī*), and sometimes into these plus a third, mixed category. The threefold division might suggest that transmitted evidence has no rational premise at all. That is false: unless the chain by which we know that reporters are truthful terminates in someone whose truthfulness is known by reason, it entails a circle or infinite regress.

Those who divide evidence into two categories mean by “transmitted” that *some premise*, near or remote, depends upon receiving testimony from a truthful speaker, and by “rational” that no premise does. Those who divide it into three mean by “transmitted” that **all immediate premises** are transmitted, as in “Pilgrimage is obligatory; everyone who omits an obligation deserves punishment.” A mixed proof has some immediate premises rational and others transmitted, as in “Ablution is an act; the legal validity of every act depends on intention,” or “Pilgrimage is obligatory; whoever omits an obligation is disobedient,” since disobedience means failing to comply with commands and prohibitions. The qualification “immediate” is vital, since even transmitted evidence ultimately rests on some rational remote premises; otherwise it would fall under the mixed category rather than standing in contrast to it.

title: Which claims require reason, transmission or both?
en:
That classification assumes evidence means *ordered premises*. If it instead refers to their **source**, as the world for knowledge of the Maker, or the Book, Sunna and consensus for legal rulings, the mixed category loses its meaning. The division then turns on whether the source's entailment of its conclusion is established by reason, in which case the evidence is rational, or otherwise by transmission.

Consider the judgement sought. If to reason the alternatives of affirmation and denial are equally open, such that reason has no independent means of choosing between them, it can only be established by report: for instance the obligation of pilgrimage or the contingent fact that Zayd is in the house. If establishing transmission itself depends on the judgement—as with knowing the speaker's truthfulness and such prerequisites as the Maker's existence, the Prophet's mission, or the evidential character of a miracle—then it must be established by reason, lest a circle arise. Otherwise it may be established either by reason or by transmission: for example the Maker's oneness or the world's origination, if a proof from the world's possibility or from the origination of accidents or certain substances can be soundly given. When rational and transmitted proofs reinforce one another, whichever first yields knowledge is what actually establishes it for the subject.

Note that transmission's dependence on the Maker's existence and the prophets' missions concerns **legal rulings**, and claims where certainty and valid proof against another person are required. For merely producing probable belief, one report or several reports thought truthful can suffice—such as sayings transmitted from certain saints, scholars or poets. Indeed, if knowledge arising from mass transmission (*tawātur*) were counted as inferential, even certain transmitted knowledge would not necessarily depend upon first establishing the Maker and the prophetic missions.

title: Why some regard transmitted evidence as incapable of yielding certainty
en:
**He says: “It is obvious that transmitted evidence yields opinion…”** The question is whether it yields knowledge. That appears to depend on knowing both that the words of the truthful reporter have been assigned the meanings understood and that the reporter intends those very meanings, so that the conclusion follows. Knowledge of linguistic assignment depends on knowing that transmitters of Arabic—vocabulary, morphology and syntax—have been protected from error and deliberate falsehood, because the assignments are learned through their testimony alone. This is clear for fundamental linguistic usages explicitly transmitted; derivative usages are based upon analogical extension of those fundamentals, an operation itself normally probable.

Knowing the speaker's intention also requires excluding several possibilities: transfer of a word to another meaning; homonymy; its figurative use outside the established meaning; an unexpressed element changing the sense; restriction of a statement apparently general in persons or times, either because only some were originally intended or because a later communication terminates a rule's duration (abrogation, *naskh*); and a rearrangement of elements that changes the apparent sense. Some of the Imām's books add the absence of *ḥadhf*, explained there as a verbal element that must be *removed* in grasping the intended sense, with Qurʾānic examples involving **لا**. Many readers take this instead to mean an element omitted from the surface wording that must be mentally supplied, distinguishing it from ellipsis (*iḍmār*) on the ground that the latter leaves a trace in the wording, such as “Welcome!” with an implicit verb of welcoming. [The exact exegetical treatment of these Qurʾānic instances requires separate verification; the distinction given here translates this text's argument, not a settled modern linguistic analysis.]

title: The rational counterargument and the limits of the sceptical argument
en:
In sum, the argument continues, one cannot be certain that all the required conditions hold and all the obstacles are absent. At most one has probability; and what rests on probable premises gives only a probable conclusion. Another indispensable condition allegedly incapable of certainty is the absence of an opposing rational argument. If such an argument exists, the transmitted text must be interpreted away from its apparent sense: one cannot assent to both a proposition and its contradictory, nor regard both contradictory claims as false. Nor may one affirm transmission while rejecting reason, since reason is transmission's foundation, upon which its authority ultimately depends. To invalidate the foundation in order to affirm the derivative would undermine both; whatever, if established, entails its own non-establishment is certainly false.

The concise text mentions only this final consideration because it is enough for the intended objection: if affirmation of the transmission requires denial of the reason upon which its warrant rests, the transmission cannot produce knowledge. Further steps are unnecessary. The purported exhaustive alternatives are in any case open to criticism. They assume that one must affirm both, reject both, or affirm one and reject the other; one may instead *suspend judgement* and regard the two arguments as cancelling each other, without affirming or denying either conclusion. If “rejecting an argument” merely means “not assenting to it,” rejecting both does not entail believing both contradictory propositions false. Failure to assent to a proof is simply failure to believe that it is sound and establishes its conclusion, not a belief in the negation of that conclusion. This may leave the investigator undecided. Moreover, rejecting both arguments would itself establish the point under consideration—the failure of transmitted evidence to produce knowledge—so excluding that alternative is redundant.

Failure to assent to a proof is simply failure to believe that it is sound and establishes its conclusion, not a belief in the negation of that conclusion. This may leave the investigator undecided. Moreover, rejecting both arguments would itself establish the point under consideration—the failure of transmitted evidence to produce knowledge—so excluding that alternative is redundant.

title: Taftāzānī's positive conclusion: transmission sometimes gives certainty
en: **The truth, however, is that transmitted evidence can yield certainty.** Some word assignments are known through mass transmission—such as “heaven” and “earth,” and most morphological and grammatical rules governing the forms of words and sentence constructions. A speaker's intention can be known with the help of contextual indicators (*qarāʾin*) that remove genuine doubt, as with texts prescribing prayer and alms, or affirming divine oneness and resurrection if transmission alone is taken as sufficient for those claims: “Say: He is God, One”; “Know that there is no god but God”; and “Say: He who produced them the first time will give them life, and He knows every creation.”

title: The possibility of a rational opponent does not always defeat certainty
en: If one objects that a rational counterargument remains possible and that its absence cannot be known with certainty from transmitted evidence, even with contextual indicators, the answer differs by subject. Knowledge that one member of an incompatible pair is established entails knowledge that its contradictory is absent, as explained earlier concerning inquiry's production of knowledge of its conclusion and the exclusion of opposing evidence.

title: Final distinction: an absent counterargument need not be known to be absent
en:
One may object that if these texts yield certainty only once we know there is no counterargument, using them to establish that absence is circular. We reply that what is thereby established is **assent that we have such knowledge**, through the establishment of what entails it. More fundamentally, the truth is that certainty requires the **absence of an opposing argument and the absence of belief that such an argument exists**, not an independently acquired cognition that no such argument exists. People frequently reach certainty by evidence without a possible opponent even entering their thoughts, whether affirmatively or negatively, much less first establishing its nonexistence. Thus when it is said that certainty comes “with knowledge of the absence of an opponent,” and that the proof supplies that knowledge, the meaning is that if reason were to attend to that alleged opponent, it would decisively reject it. This is confirmed by the argument used for the requirement: a genuine opponent would defeat firm assent and produce suspension of judgement. Reflect upon this; God is the guide.

title: Why general matters form a separate division
en: **On the words, “The Second Objective.”** We have already indicated that this objective is placed before the remaining four because the exposition of some of their questions depends upon it. The reason for separating it from them, although it is connected with them, is as follows. Inquiry concerns the states of the existent (*al-mawjūd*). The existent is divided into the necessary being (*al-wājib*), substance (*jawhar*), and accident (*ʿaraḍ*), each of which possesses states treated in its proper division. A distinct division was therefore needed for those states common to all three, such as existence and unity, or to only two, such as origination and multiplicity. Hence, when people say that “general matters” are what encompass “most existents,” the intended existents are the three divisions—the necessary, substance, and accident—not all the individual things that belong to them. The intellect cannot enumerate these individuals, identify a majority among them, or decide that causality and multiplicity, for example, pertain to most of those individuals.

title: The scope of the general-matters division
en: Clearly, what is intended for consideration here is what serves a scientific purpose, advances a principal aim of the discipline, and is not treated as a primary subject in one of the other objectives. Otherwise numerous very widespread features would have to be discussed here although they are not: quantity, quality, relation, being knowable, being subject to power, the various questions concerning the five universals, essential definition and description, position, predication, and indeed most second intelligibles (*al-maʿqūlāt al-thāniya*). Nor does it matter that some of these are purely considerational or are not restricted to existents, for some of the subjects actually investigated here have precisely these features, as does possibility (*imkān*).

title: Nonexistence, impossibility, necessity, and eternity
en: **Objection:** Some investigations concern what does not encompass existents at all, such as impossibility and nonexistence; others concern what undoubtedly belongs only to the necessary being, such as necessity and eternity (*qidam*). **Reply:** Since the inquiry is confined in its primary intention to states of the existent, nonexistence and impossibility are discussed incidentally, as opposites of existence and possibility. Necessity and eternity are discussed insofar as they belong to the divisions of necessity and eternity taken without qualification: necessary existence, whether through itself or through another, and absence of being preceded by nonexistence. In these general senses they are widely applicable. The point is evident for necessity; for eternity it holds according to the philosophers, who assert the eternity of immaterial things, motion, time, and other substances and accidents. The discipline of kalām examines that [latter assertion] by way of negation, not affirmation: it denies that such eternity belongs among general matters, rather as the question of a *ḥāl* is treated by someone who denies the existence of such states.

title: Chapter 1 and the immediacy of conceiving existence
en: **On the words, “The First Chapter.”** The second objective is arranged in three chapters, concerning existence, quiddity, and their concomitants. The first also includes investigation of nonexistence. The truth is that the conception (*taṣawwur*) of existence is self-evident (*badīhī*), and that this very judgement is likewise self-evident: anyone who attends to it can be certain of it, even without having practiced the methods of acquiring knowledge. Most philosophers consequently say that nothing is better known than existence. They appeal to induction, which suffices for this claim: if the intellect finds among its intelligibles nothing more familiar than existence, or even anything on its level, existence is established as the clearest thing to the intellect.

title: Nominal explanation is not a real definition
en: A meaning that is already clear may nevertheless be identified as the signification of one expression rather than another. It may therefore receive a **verbal or nominal explanation** (*taʿrīf lafẓī*), which enables someone to understand it through that expression, without purporting to furnish the very conception of the meaning in itself. Were it to do the latter, it would involve circularity or the definition of a thing by itself. This is the role of explaining *wujūd* by “being” (*kawn*), “establishment” (*thubūt*), “actuality” (*taḥaqquq*), “thingness” (*shayʾiyya*), “obtaining” (*ḥuṣūl*), and expressions of the kind, for someone who knows the sense of existence through these terms but not yet through the word *wujūd*. If the situation were reversed, the direction of the nominal explanation would likewise be reversed.

title: Descriptive definitions and circularity
en: Consider, by contrast, defining existence as “what is established in itself” (*al-thābit al-ʿayn*), “that about which one can make a statement and which can be known,” “that which divides into agent and patient,” or “that which divides into eternal and originated.” If the intention is to offer a real descriptive definition (*rasm*), its circularity is clear. One cannot understand “that which is established,” “that which is possible,” and expressions of this kind without already conceiving obtaining in the external things themselves or in minds. Even granting otherwise, the concept of existence is plainly clearer to the intellect than the senses conveyed by these expressions.

title: An attempted distinction between the established and the existent

title: Two interpretations of the first argument
en: **Reply:** If the claim is that this judgement is self-evident together with **all its objects and constituents**, in accordance with the Imām's account of assent (*taṣdīq*), the claim is denied. If the claim is only that the act of judgement itself is self-evident, meaning that, once the objects of judgement have been conceived, the judgement requires no acquisition, that is conceded. But it does not prove the proposition at issue: that existence is conceived in its reality without acquisition. A judgement may be immediate even when its subject and predicate are grasped only under some aspect, not in their full realities, and even when conceiving them requires acquisition.

title: Second argument: existence is not susceptible of essential definition
en:
**Second argument:** Existence is known in its reality. Knowledge of it must arise either immediately or through acquisition, and acquisition is by essential definition (*ḥadd*) or descriptive definition (*rasm*). This is an argument against those who admit these premises; hence the Imām does not stop to defend them. But existence cannot be acquired by essential definition, for such definition belongs to a composite, whereas existence is not composite. If it were, its constituents would either be existences or things other than existences. If they were existences, the thing would precede itself and a part would equal the whole in the entirety of its quiddity—both impossible. The first impossibility is plain. As for the second, a part enters into the quiddity of the whole, whereas it does not enter into its own quiddity in that way.

This consequence presupposes that **absolute existence**, which is said hypothetically to be composite, is not outside particular existences: it must either be identical with their quiddities, yielding the second impossibility, or be an essential constituent of them, yielding the first. Otherwise the parts could be particular existences, either identical with particular quiddities or superadded to them, while absolute existence lies outside those quiddities, and neither impossibility follows. But if the parts are **not** existences, then either some additional thing—existence itself—arises when they come together or it does not. If no such thing arises, existence would consist entirely in what is not existence, which is impossible. If it does arise, composition would belong not to existence itself, which is that additional accidental feature, but to the subject bearing it. That contradicts the hypothesis.

title: Al-Rāzī's formulation and the objection to descriptive definition
en:
The Imām's formulation in the *Mabāḥith* is this: if existence were composite and its constituents were existent in character, one existence would be many existences. If they were not existent in character, either their conjunction would give rise to no attribute of existence, so that existence would be a collection of nonexistential things, or it would give rise to such an attribute. In the latter case, the collection would either produce that existence or receive it; the composition would thus belong to its producer or recipient, not to existence itself.

Nor, according to the argument, can existence be acquired by *rasm*. As previously claimed, such a description conveys information only after one knows that the distinguishing extrinsic characteristic belongs specifically to the thing described; but knowing this already requires knowing the thing, and so is circular. Moreover, one would need to know distinctly that it belongs to that thing rather than the others, which is impossible on the argument. Even if granted, such a description would not disclose the thing's reality.

In the latter case, the collection would either produce that existence or receive it; the composition would thus belong to its producer or recipient, not to existence itself.

Nor, according to the argument, can existence be acquired by rasm. As previously claimed, such a description conveys information only after one knows that the distinguishing extrinsic characteristic belongs specifically to the thing described; but knowing this already requires knowing the thing, and so is circular. Moreover, one would need to know distinctly that it belongs to that thing rather than the others, which is impossible on the argument. Even if granted, such a description would not disclose the thing's reality.

title: Counterexample to the argument against composite existence
en: The reply to the first formulation of the alleged impossibility of existence being composite is by **counterexample** (*naqḍ*). If all its premises were valid, no quiddity whatsoever could be composite, for the reasoning can be repeated with any composite. Consider a house. Either its constituents are themselves houses, which is impossible, or they are not houses. If they are not, either a further thing arises from their conjunction and is the house—in which case composition would not be in the house, contrary to the hypothesis—or no further thing arises, in which case a house would consist entirely of things that are not houses.

title: Intellectual composition and the predication of existence
en: **Reply:** The solution is what we have already indicated: the constituents may themselves be **existences**, meaning things of which “existence” is predicated as an accidental predicate is predicated of its subject. title: The first objection to the self-evidence of existence
en:
**On the words, “If it is said.”** He intends to set out the arguments used by those who deny that existence is self-evident, together with their replies. **First:** existence is either identical with quiddity or additional to it. If identical with quiddity, since quiddities are not self-evident, existence cannot be self-evident. If additional, it is an accident of quiddity—that is what additionality means—and must therefore depend upon its substrates in intelligibility. An accident has no independence apart from the subject in which it is found. Since those substrates are not self-evident, the existence that is accidental to them is not self-evident either, a fortiori.

Do not object that the discussion concerns **absolute existence**, not the particular existences that are accidental to quiddities; or that, even if absolute existence is an accident, it is accidental only to **absolute quiddity**, whereas the quiddities known through acquisition are particular quiddities. On that view, absolute existence's being an accident would not require it to depend upon those acquired particular quiddities. We reply that absolute existence is itself an accident of particular existences, as will be explained. It consequently depends upon them, while they depend upon the particular quiddities known through acquisition; absolute existence therefore depends on those quiddities **through an intermediary**. This is what is meant by its increased dependence. Likewise, absolute quiddity is an accident of particular quiddities, being predicable of them without constituting them. It thus depends upon them, and absolute existence, as an accident of absolute quiddity, is an accident of those particular quiddities through an intermediary.

title: Response to the first objection: intellectual and external inherence
en:
**Reply to the first:** We deny that an accident must depend upon its substrate **for being intelligible**; an accident can sometimes be conceived without conceiving its substrate. Its lack of independent subsistence applies to its **realization in external things**. Even granting the point, nobody disputes that certain quiddities are themselves immediately conceived, and these are enough for the conception of existence without acquisition.

Do not argue: an accident depends upon its substrate for its realization **wherever** it is accidental; if its accidentality is external, the dependence is external, and if its accidentality is intellectual, the dependence must be intellectual. It will be explained that existence is added to quiddity only in intellect. What is conceived together with a self-evident quiddity would accordingly be that quiddity's **particular existence**, whereas absolute existence is not essential to particular existence such that its self-evidence must follow; it is merely accidental to it.

We reply that “being accidental in the intellect” does **not** mean that the accident cannot be realized in the intellect without its substrate, inhering in that substrate as an external accident inheres in its subject. Rather, it means that when the intellect considers the two things and their relationship, what it conceives of one is not identical with, nor a constituent of, what it conceives of the other, although one is truly predicable of the other. Absolute existence, even though it is not essential to particular existence, is indisputably inseparable from it. That concomitance is present only in the intellect, since there is no corresponding distinction in external reality. Particular existence cannot therefore be conceived without absolute existence, and the latter is as self-evident as the former.

en:
Another argument is that, if existence could be conceived, there would be impressed in the soul a form corresponding to it. Since the soul already possesses existence, two things alike would coexist. Even granting that point, we deny that pure negation cannot be conceived. title: Three disputed theses about existence
en:
**On the words, “The second investigation.”** What is transmitted from Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī is that the existence of each thing is identical with its essence, and that the term *existence* has no one concept common to the different existences: the sharing is merely verbal. According to the majority, however, it has one concept shared by the existences. The theologians nevertheless hold that existence is one reality diversified by qualifications and relations: even the Necessary Existent's existence is His being in concrete reality, just as one understands the being of a human being; the difference is in quiddity. Existence is accordingly a meaning additional to quiddity in the Necessary and in the possible alike. According to the philosophers, by contrast, the Necessary Existent's existence differs in reality from possible existence. Their sharing in the concept of being is the sharing of two subjects in a nonconstitutive, extrinsic concomitant. For a possible thing existence is additional to its quiddity in the intellect, whereas for the Necessary it is the essence itself: the Necessary has no quiddity beyond the particular existence that is free from conjunction with a quiddity. A human being, on the other hand, has a quiddity—rational animal—and an existence, namely being in concrete reality.

The investigation therefore takes place at three points: (1) whether *existence* is shared in meaning; (2) whether it is additional in the mind; and (3) whether it is additional even in the Necessary. Fairness requires acknowledging that the first two are self-evident. What has been advanced as proof is better understood as calling attention to them. The first thesis can be illuminated in several ways.
