On the words, “The second investigation.” What is transmitted from Shaykh Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī is that the existence of each thing is identical with its essence, and that the term existence has no one concept common to the different existences: the sharing is merely verbal. According to the majority, however, it has one concept shared by the existences. The theologians nevertheless hold that existence is one reality diversified by qualifications and relations: even the Necessary Existent's existence is His being in concrete reality, just as one understands the being of a human being; the difference is in quiddity. Existence is accordingly a meaning additional to quiddity in the Necessary and in the possible alike. According to the philosophers, by contrast, the Necessary Existent's existence differs in reality from possible existence. Their sharing in the concept of being is the sharing of two subjects in a nonconstitutive, extrinsic concomitant. For a possible thing existence is additional to its quiddity in the intellect, whereas for the Necessary it is the essence itself: the Necessary has no quiddity beyond the particular existence that is free from conjunction with a quiddity. A human being, on the other hand, has a quiddity—rational animal—and an existence, namely being in concrete reality.

The investigation therefore takes place at three points: (1) whether existence is shared in meaning; (2) whether it is additional in the mind; and (3) whether it is additional even in the Necessary. Fairness requires acknowledging that the first two are self-evident. What has been advanced as proof is better understood as calling attention to them. The first thesis can be illuminated in several ways.

title: First indication: a certain judgment amid changing hypotheses
en: **First:** When we consider an originated thing, we know with certainty that it has an agent or cause, while remaining uncertain whether that cause is necessary or possible, accident or substance, spatially located or not spatially located. Our belief about its being possible may even change into a belief that it is necessary, and similar changes can occur concerning other particular descriptions. Necessarily, what remains the certain object of judgment while those descriptions remain doubtful and our beliefs about them change must be something common to all of them.

title: Second indication: the subject divided is common to its divisions
en:
**Second:** We divide *existent* into necessary and possible. What is subjected to a division is common to the things that fall under it. There is no meaning to dividing a thing except into some of the things of which it is predicable. Thus to say, “An animal is either white or not white,” divides animal into white animals and the others; it does not divide it into whiteness taken without restriction—which would include nonanimal things—and something else. Even if that were granted, it would not damage our purpose. Our purpose is simply to establish something shared between necessary and possible being against those who deny any sharing whatever; or one might say that no one maintains that it is shared by these two while denying that it is shared by the other possible beings. Alternatively, this division guides us toward proving its generality: the existent which is possible is either substance or accident, and a substance is either human or nonhuman, and so on.

**Objection to the first two indications:** Why could the certain content that remains be the realization of one among the several meanings of the expression *existence*, without a single universal concept? Why should the division not merely list the meanings of a homonymous expression, as one says, “An *ʿayn* is either a flowing spring or a seeing eye,” rather than enumerate the divisions of a universal concept? **Reply:** We find the certainty of this judgment and the correctness of the division even when we set aside naming conventions, language, and the word *existence* altogether.

A further counterexample is proposed from *quiddity* and *individuation*. We remain sure that the cause of an originated thing has a quiddity and an individuation while uncertain whether it is necessary or possible; both quiddity and individuation admit division into necessary and possible. Yet no particular quiddity or particular individuation is shared by them all. The answer is that unrestricted *quiddity* and unrestricted *individuation* are themselves universal concepts shared by the respective particular quiddities and individuations. Hence there is no counterexample. It would be an objection only if we had claimed that all existences were equal in reality, so that the concept of existence was their very essence. Plainly none of these indications establishes that stronger claim.

title: Third and fourth indications: the division of existent and nonexistent
en:
**Third:** If existence had no common concept, the exhaustive division into existent and nonexistent would fail. For suppose we said that a human being has existence in one of the meanings of that term or else is nonexistent: the intellect could still allow that the human is existent in some *other* meaning, and the exclusion of that possibility would require its own argument. This difficulty does not depend upon nonexistence's having one concept; if it had several, the failure of exhaustiveness would be more obvious still, since the thing could be nonexistent in another sense. We have therefore departed from those who reason that nonexistence has one concept, so that unless its opposite had one concept the rational exhaustive division would fail.

We make the unity of the concept of nonexistence a **fourth** indication. Nonexistence has one concept; if existence lacked one concept, existence and nonexistence would not be contradictories, since both could be absent where existence is taken in some other meaning. The consequence is plainly false. **Objection:** We do not concede that nonexistence has a single concept: existence is the very reality of each thing, and nonexistence is its removal, so every existence has its corresponding removal. **Reply:** Whether the negation concerns existence in the sense of a shared being or the particular reality itself, the concept of negation is necessarily one; its multiplicity is only by relation to different objects. **Further objection:** Non-human, non-horse, and non-tree evidently have distinct concepts. If *nonexistence* is assigned to each, how can its meaning be one? **Reply:** All share the concept expressed by the negating particle “not.” That is what nonexistence means here, and nothing beyond this shared concept is intended by saying it is one.

title: Five indications that existence and quiddity differ conceptually
en:
**On the words, “And concerning the second [thesis].”** Five considerations direct attention to existence's additionality over quiddity: they are compatible with existence but incompatible with the quiddity and its constitutive elements.

**(1) Possibility of negation.** One can negate existence of a quiddity, as in “The phoenix does not exist”; one cannot negate a quiddity, or any of its constitutive elements, of that quiddity itself. **(2) Informative predication.** Predicating existence of a quiddity known through and through conveys information not already contained in knowing the quiddity. Predicating the quiddity itself, or its constitutive elements, does not. **(3) Acquisition of assent.** Assent that existence belongs to a given quiddity may require investigation and an acquired proof, as in the existence of the jinn; assent that the quiddity and its essential constituents belong to themselves does not. **(4) Unity of concept.** The existence of a human, horse, and tree has one concept—being in concrete reality—whereas their quiddities differ in concept. **(5) Separability in intellection.** We may conceive a quiddity without conceiving that it exists. The point is obvious in external existence. As regards mental existence, we do not know, simply by the act of conception, that conception is existence in the intellect. Even if that were granted, it is established only by argument. Even granting that, the conception of a thing need not include cognizance of one's conception of it. Even granting that also, it may be possible for something to exist externally that we do not apprehend at all. Furthermore, we may assent that a quiddity and its essentials belong to that quiddity—in the sense that it is what it is—without assenting that it has external or mental existence. The expression “in intellection” has deliberately been preferred so as to embrace conception and assent together.

Many writers say instead: “We conceive the quiddity of a triangle while doubting its external and mental existence.” The difficulty with that formulation is that it does not establish the intended result: it says that we apprehend the quiddity by way of conception but fail to apprehend existence by way of assent, and that distinction is compatible with the alleged identity of the two. These five considerations are indications against the view that what is understood by a thing's existence is exactly what is understood by the thing itself. Some apply to Necessary and possible being alike; some concern possibles in general; still others particular possible cases. It is accordingly mistaken to object that a given consideration does not prove additionality for Necessary and possible being together, or that a particular example cannot prove a universal rule. Equally, none of them purports to establish that existence and quiddity are distinct *entities* rather than distinct *concepts*.

title: Philosophers' three arguments against additionality in the Necessary
en:
**On the words, “The philosophers objected.”** The philosophers contend that the existence of the Necessary cannot be additional to its quiddity; otherwise one of three impossibilities follows: (1) one and the same thing would be both recipient and producer of existence, whose impossibility is to be explained later; (2) the thing would have to precede its own existence *by existing*, which is manifestly impossible. There is no need to add the Imām's further argument that it would give the thing two existences and lead to an infinite regress: if the prior existence were the quiddity itself, the philosopher's thesis would already be granted; otherwise the same question recurs indefinitely; (3) the Necessary's existence would be able to depart from it, equally an impossibility.

The reasoning for **(1)** is that the quiddity would be receptive of existence by supposition and productive of it by entailment. For **(2)**, existence, as an accident, would depend upon quiddity as its subject, and therefore be possible, since it depends upon another. Its cause would have to be the quiddity itself, not some other thing, since the Necessary's existence cannot depend on another; and every cause precedes its effect, so quiddity would precede its own existence in existence. For **(3)**, existence dependent upon another would be possible and could, considered in itself, cease; otherwise it would be necessary through itself, contrary to the supposition. The qualification “considered in itself” answers the reply that not every possible thing may cease, since a possible thing necessary through another cannot cease so long as that necessitating other remains.

The reply to **(1)** is that the impossibility of one thing's being both recipient and producer is not conceded; its proof is discussed later. The reply to **(2)** denies that quiddity must precede existence *by existing*. That would follow only if the cause had to precede its effect by existence in every case, and that is disputed. What is necessary is that the cause precede by whatever constitutes its causality: if by existence, then by existence; if by its quiddity, then by quiddity. The necessary concomitants grounded in quiddity itself illustrate this: the quiddity of three precedes oddness precisely as that quiddity, without consideration of its being existent or nonexistent. Likewise the receiver necessarily precedes what it receives; yet this precedence can be by quiddity alone, as with the quiddities of possibles in relation to their existence. The reply to **(3)** denies that existence dependent upon quiddity must on that account be capable, in itself, of leaving it. That follows only if the quiddity does not of itself require existence. To be Necessary Existent is simply for the thing's existence to be unable, considered in relation to its essence, to depart. Its existence's dependence upon that very essence does not damage the designation, even if one could, outside proper technical usage, call it possible under that description: the possible, technically speaking, requires *another* for the establishment of existence. That is why the concise text mentions dependence rather than possibility.

title: Whether a cause of its own existence must first exist
en:
**On the words, “If it be said.”** The philosophers' decisive case is the second one. The Imām's reply amounts to asking why the cause of existence might not be the quiddity *as such*, preceding it not by existence, just as a quiddity's constituents precede it without themselves first existing, and a quiddity is the cause of its concomitants through itself rather than through its existence. Equally, possible quiddity receives its existence, though a receiver must in some sense precede what is received. The critical philosopher [*al-ḥakīm al-muḥaqqiq*, attribution requiring checking] answers in several works that the issue concerns a cause of the existence of something externally existing. Intellectual self-evidence requires such a cause to be prior in existence: unless a thing is considered existent it cannot be considered a source or bestower of existence. The recipient of existence is different: the intellect must consider it apart from existence, lest the thing already obtained be obtained again, and apart even from nonexistence, lest contradictories coincide. What is thus conceived is the quiddity taken in itself. The essentials in relation to quiddity, and a quiddity in relation to its own concomitants, need precede only in *intellectual* existence, since their priority and attribution belong to intellectual consideration. The receptive subject of existence is therefore similarly prior only in intellectual consideration; it is not like the body on which whiteness is present.

We reply by way of dialectical inquiry, not by asserting a final demonstration: we do not concede that what bestows **its own** existence must precede that existence by being existent. Its bestowal means only that its quiddity requires existence through itself, and, just as in the case of the receptive subject, its already existing beforehand would be impossible, since that would obtain what was already obtained. A bestower of existence on **another** is different: intellectual self-evidence requires it first to exist, since without existing it cannot be the origin of another's existence. This is how the world is used to infer the Maker's existence.

**Objection:** If the Necessary's quiddity produces and necessitates its existence, then that existence is an effect of something other than itself. Every such effect is possible; so the Necessary's existence would be possible—contradiction. **Reply:** Even if we accept calling something entailed by quiddity its *effect* and calling the existing essence something *other than* its existence, we deny that every effect of another in this broadened sense is possible. Such a conclusion would follow only if the effect were not existence and the “other” were not the very quiddity in which that existence subsists. The necessity of existence consists precisely in being required by the essence in which it subsists, without needing anything beyond that essence. This is what the text's reply “through its essence” means: the Necessary's existence must be required by the Necessary's essence, and hence necessity rather than possibility follows. More precisely, to say that a quiddity is necessary means that by itself it requires existence; to say that its existence is necessary means that it is required by that quiddity without any need for something else. Whether we say “necessary of existence through itself” or “existence necessary through itself,” the intended referent is the essence of the existent, not an essence belonging to existence considered independently.

One cannot avoid the difficulty by saying that independence merely requires the absence of what entails conjunction: it would still depend upon that absence. The reply is that independence belongs to the essence of the **particular** existence of the Necessary, which is really different from all other existences.

title: Second counterargument: sourcehood of possibles
en: **Second:** The Necessary is the principle of possible beings. If the Necessary were a bare existence, either being their principle would belong to that existence through itself, making every existence a principle in the same way. That is impossible: Zayd's existence cannot be the cause of itself and of its own causes. Or this principle would be existence **together with** the qualification of independence, making the principle composite; worse, one of the components, independence or abstraction, is negative, so the purported principle would not be an existent whole. Or it would be existence **on condition that** it be independent, in which case every existence could in itself be a principle of every other existence, lacking the status merely through failure of a condition. But a thing's being a principle of itself or of its own causes is intrinsically impossible, not something prevented merely by the absence of a condition of principality. The reply is that the Necessary is a principle through its own essence, which is a particular existence differing in reality from the other existences. It does not follow that all existences have this property.

title: Fourth counterargument: bare being, abstraction, and composition
en: **Fourth:** If the Necessary were identical with being in concrete reality, understood as unrestricted existence, there would be a plurality of Necessary Existents, since Zayd's existence differs from ʿAmr's. If He were being together with the qualification of being abstracted from quiddity, He would be composite of being and abstraction, although abstraction is a negation and cannot constitute a component of the Necessary. If He were being **under the condition** of abstraction, He would not be necessary through Himself but through a condition, namely abstraction. If He differed from being in concrete reality, either He would be without that being—which is impossible, since existence without being is unintelligible—or He would have it. title: Fifth counterargument and the Imām's species-nature objection
en:
**Fifth:** Existence is known by necessity, whereas all agree that the Necessary's reality is not known. What is known cannot be identical with what is unknown. The reply is that what is known is unrestricted existence, which differs from the particular existence constituting that reality. The text points to all these replies in saying that there is no dispute about the unrestricted existence being additional to the Necessary's quiddity. What is disputed is whether His **particular existence** is additional; the arguments advanced do not establish this.

**On the words, “If it be said.”** The Imām [al-Rāzī] has another objection which is not answered simply by the preceding distinction. Existence is a specific nature (*ṭabīʿa nawʿiyya*), since you have maintained that it has one concept common to everything. A specific nature cannot have different necessary concomitants: whatever belongs to one of its individuals must belong to the others, since what an essence entails cannot fail to follow from that essence. Many of your rules are built on this principle. If existence entails inherence in another or its absence, that consequence must apply equally to necessary and possible existence. If it entails neither, the Necessary would depend upon something extrinsic for His necessity, as before.

title: Univocal and analogical commonness, and the attribution to al-Rāzī
en:
**On the words, “Whether univocally or by gradation.”** The preceding denial is sufficient: things differing in their essences may share a single nonessential concomitant, whether it is predicated of them equally or univocally (*bi-l-tawāṭuʾ*), as *quiddity* of different quiddities and *individuation* of different individuations, or with priority, perfection, or intensity (*bi-l-tashkīk*), as whiteness and heat of their diverse instances. It does not follow from existence's being one common concept that existence is a specific nature whose instances agree in real constitution and necessary concomitants. We could make the point even if existence were predicated equally of all, without gradation. Nevertheless, the actual mode is predication by gradation; and the critical philosopher habitually seeks the precise account rather than the merely sufficient refutation. He therefore says that existence is predicated of existences by gradation: it is prior in the cause to what is in the effect, belongs more properly to substance than accident, and is more intensive in an enduring accident such as blackness than in one that does not endure, such as movement. Above all, Necessary existence is prior, more proper, and more intensive than possible existence.

What is predicated of things with such gradation is a nonconstitutive attribute external to their essences, not their essence or a constituent of it, since essence and essential constituents cannot differ in that manner, as will be explained. Existence is therefore not the specific nature of particular existences, but an extrinsic concomitant truly predicable in one meaning of its various subjects. Their agreement under this one concomitant does not entail that its subjects—Necessary existence and the existences of possible things—agree in real constitution. There is therefore no impossibility in their differing as to inherence or non-inherence, being a principle of possible beings or not, and similar features.

It is surprising that the Imām had read in al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā that, for them, the Necessary's reality is pure particular existence, independent of any quiddity [the immediately following words in the electronic text are damaged and are left for printed-image collation], while the familiar unrestricted concept of existence is its concomitant rather than a constituent. The whole difficulty is that he did not distinguish equality **under one concept** from equality **in reality**. title: What analogical predication does and does not establish
en:
**On the words, “So it is additional to them.”** This rejects a misunderstanding of the preceding discussion. Some had thought that if existence is predicated by gradation, it must be additional **in every instance**, which is exactly what the theologians wanted to establish. They reasoned that, if predicated equally, differences in inherence and non-inherence are impossible, while, if predicated by gradation, those differences also fail, because graded predication itself entails the additionality of existence everywhere. Both claims are false. The first fails because something predicated equally may still be a nonessential attribute of subjects differing in their essences and concomitants. The second fails because graded predication implies only that the **common concept** is additional to the **particular existences falling under it**. That is not the thesis requiring proof. The disputed additionality is whether each particular existence is itself an accident of a quiddity, subsisting in it intellectually. The first does not imply the second: one subject of the graded or common concept *existence* may be self-subsisting existence—subsisting through itself and giving subsistence to other things—because its reality differs from the others.

The Imām expresses surprise: how can the accident so weak that, as a merely relational notion of being in concrete reality, it cannot stand independently in conception or predication, suddenly become, in the case of the Necessary, a self-subsisting essence independent of a cause and the foundation of the independence of every independent thing? More surprising still, responds al-Taftāzānī, is that such a remark should proceed from an Imām of his stature.

**On the next objection:** If existence were not a specific nature constituting the complete reality of the existents, the individual existences would be wholly disparate; they could not share any constitutive element, since Necessary existence cannot be composite. This is supposed to contradict the established meaningful sharing of existence. **Reply:** If disparity means that the particular existences are not predicable of one another, we deny that this is impossible: their participation in a common concept does not entail that the particular existences are predicable of one another. If disparity means that they share nothing at all, we deny that this follows. Failure to share an entire reality or an essential constituent does not exclude their sharing an **accidental predicate**, the concept of being. In the same manner individuals and species of walking animals share the concept *walking* without being predicable of one another.

title: The argument that existence cannot be an accident of quiddity
en: **On the words, “And the Shaykh maintained.”** Those who say that existence is identical with quiddity both for the Necessary and for possible things offer several arguments. Their common point is this: if existence were not the very quiddity—and no one holds that it is a constituent of quiddity—it would be additional to it, inhering in it as a quality in a qualified subject. Yet the inherence of one thing in another presupposes that both possess establishment in themselves, since what has no being of its own can be neither a subject nor something subsisting in a subject. This assumption yields impossibilities from either side, quiddity or existence. As for quiddity, were it established as the receptive subject of existence, either it would be established by the same existence, in which case the thing would precede itself, since the subject's existence necessarily precedes an accident; or it would be established by another existence, producing an infinite regress, since that second existence would itself be accidental and require the prior existence of its subject. As for existence, if it is itself established, while the very establishment of each thing is supposed to be additional to that thing, then an infinite regress of existences results. By dividing the cases according to existence and nonexistence, both for the receptive subject and for what inheres in it, the difficulty is expressed in four arguments.

title: The first two regress or contradiction arguments
en:
**First:** If existence inheres in quiddity while quiddity without existence is nonexistent, existence would inhere in the nonexistent. The thing would be described by both existence and nonexistence, a contradiction.

**Second:** If existence inhered in quiddity, quiddity would need to precede it in being, as is the case with other subjects and their accidents. If it preceded it through the very existence under discussion, there would be circularity: the inherence of existence would depend upon the quiddity's existing, while its existing would depend upon existence inhering in it. If it preceded existence by a different existence, an infinite regress would follow, since the second existence, too, would be an accident presupposing some earlier existence of its subject, and so on. It has been said that this regress, besides being impossible by arguments to be given later and because it would confine an infinity between the two present termini of quiddity and existence, itself proves the intended conclusion that existence is identical with quiddity. If *all* the added existences inhere in quiddity, the quiddity must possess an existence not itself additional, for otherwise the collection would not be the whole collection. There is a difficulty in this response: on the supposition of an infinite regress, we do not concede the existence of a completed totality beyond which no further existence remains. Whatever totality is posited, its subject would have an additional existence beyond it. That is what an endless regress of this sort means: there is no terminus in an existence beyond which another existence does not intervene between it and quiddity.

title: Third and fourth arguments; their reduction to two dilemmas
en:
**Third:** If a thing's existence were additional to it, existence itself would not be existent, since the regress of existences is impossible. It would therefore be nonexistent, which would make something possess its own contradictory and make what has no establishment in itself established within its subject.

**Fourth:** If existence inhere in quiddity, it must be existent: a thing cannot be described by its contradictory, and something without its own establishment cannot be established in a subject. We may then ask about *its* existence, and an infinite regress follows, because by supposition the existence of each thing is additional to it.

On careful analysis these four arguments reduce to two dilemmas, according to the alternatives of existence and nonexistence on the side of the subject and on the side of the accident, as set out in the concise text. The **first** asks: if existence inheres in quiddity, is the quiddity taken as subject nonexistent, in which case a contradiction follows, or existent, in which case either circularity or regress follows? The **second** asks: is the existence that inheres itself nonexistent, in which case the subject is described by the opposite of existence and a thing without self-establishment is established in another, or existent, in which case its own existence must be added and the sequence of existences proceeds endlessly?

title: General reply: additionality is intellectual, not external inherence
en:
The **general reply** is that existence's additionality over quiddity, and its subsisting in quiddity, are spoken of **according to the intellect**: the intellect can consider either without expressly considering the other, and regards existence as a meaning related particularly to quiddity. It is not an external inherence in the manner in which a body's whiteness subsists in that body. The alleged impossibilities follow only on that false construal.

The **detailed reply to the first dilemma** is that existence subsists in quiddity *as such*, neither in a nonexistent quiddity so as to generate a contradiction nor in an already existent quiddity so as to create a circle or infinite regress. **Objection:** If “quiddity as such” means merely that existence and nonexistence are not identical with the quiddity or its constituent parts, that does not help: inherence alone still generates the impossibilities. If it means that the quiddity is neither existent nor nonexistent, whether through accident or otherwise, its contradiction is even more manifest, since nonexistence is the contradictory of existence. **Reply:** It means quiddity considered *without including either existence or nonexistence among the considerations applied to it*, although in external reality it cannot be separated from the one or the other.

**Further objection:** That inseparability is enough for the difficulty. If the quiddity is accompanied by nonexistence, contradiction follows; if by existence, circle or regress follows. **Reply:** The inherence of existence in quiddity is an intellectual matter and is not like that of whiteness in a body. The quiddity therefore need not precede it with an ontological or temporal priority in existence. At most it has to precede through intellectual existence, and that is not impossible: the quiddity can be considered by itself without simultaneously considering its external or mental existence, while having an intellectual existence that is not itself expressly considered. Not taking something into consideration is different from considering its nonexistence. If the intellect goes on expressly to consider the quiddity's mental existence, a regress need not ensue; the series ends wherever intellectual consideration ends. Those denying mental existence may instead simply deny that a subject must invariably precede its accident in existence: such priority holds for accidents of an existent, not for properties attributed to quiddity as quiddity.

title: Detailed reply: existence need not have a second existence
en:
Against the **second dilemma**, one may accept that existence is existent but deny that its existence must in turn be added to it. That would follow only if existence's own existence were additional; it is not. The debate concerns things other than existence. Since every thing's obtaining is through existence, existence itself necessarily obtains through itself, without requiring another existence inhering in it. Likewise, because other things are temporally prior or posterior through time, the priority and posteriority of the parts of time are intrinsic to time itself and do not require a second time.

**Objection:** This would make every existence necessary, since necessary existence supposedly means nothing except obtaining through oneself. **Reply:** The senses are different. The Necessary Existent exists through itself in the sense that its essence requires existence without needing a producing cause. The existence of a possible thing, when it has been given either by its own essence—as in the Necessary—or by another—as in the possible—does not require *yet another existence* for that existence to obtain. A human, by contrast, is an existent after the action of its cause and by means of an existence intellectually attributed to it. Moreover, saying “things obtain by means of existence” is itself a concession to ordinary usage: existence is the *obtaining of things*, not a distinct instrument by which they obtain. The intended meaning is that things obtain when the intellect attributes existence to them and they are identical with it in external reality.

Alternatively, we may choose the claim that existence is **not itself an existent**, without admitting that it is therefore characterized by its opposite. The contradictory of *existence* is *nonexistence*, or *not-existence*, not the noun *a nonexistent* or *something non-existent*. At most it follows that existence is not **a possessor of existence**, just as blackness is not itself **a possessor of blackness**; and that is correct. Nor does it follow that a thing with no external establishment subsists externally in a subject. As already explained, existence's relation to quiddity is intellectual, not external like whiteness in a body; only its being cognized in the intellect follows.

title: Inadequate replies and the real basis for rejecting the objections
en: One proposed reply to the first dilemma is to turn it against accidents of subjects, such as a body's blackness. Does blackness inhere in a body already black? Then one faces circularity, regress, or the conjunction of two like things. Does it inhere in a not-black body? Then one faces contradiction. This is a weak counterexample. Blackness inheres in a body that becomes black **through this very blackness**, not through a blackness already in it. When blackness supervenes on a previously nonblack body, the body becomes black at that very moment, without contradiction. The analogy fails in the case of existence and quiddity because the opponent's claim precisely is that a subject's precedence over its accident **in existence** is necessary. The subject cannot first be existent through the very existence now supposed to inhere in it. title: Reconciliation of the schools: concept versus identity
en:
**On the words, “If you say.”** The author seeks to state the views of the Shaykh and of the theologians and philosophers in a way consistent with intellectual self-evidence. On a superficial reading the Shaykh seems to say that *the existence of a human being* means *rational animal*, for instance, and that the Arabic term *wujūd*, the Persian *hastī*, and their counterparts in other languages are homonyms with indefinitely numerous meanings corresponding to the different existents. The theologians appear to say that existence is an accident inhering in quiddity just as other accidents inhere in their subjects. The philosophers appear to say that this is so of possibles, whereas in the Necessary existence is some other, intellectually inaccessible meaning. All of these interpretations are evidently false.

The author of *al-Ṣaḥāʾif* traces the disagreement to two senses of the word *existence*: the concept of being and that of essence. One party, calling existence additional to quiddity, intends being; the other, calling it identical with quiddity, intends essence. Once this is explained the disagreement disappears. This account is defective for three reasons. **First**, the arguments of both parties expressly concern existence as the opposite of nonexistence, that is, being. **Second**, the concept of essence itself is one meaning common to essences, so this interpretation does not explain why existence could be shared by existences without homonymy or a plurality of linguistic conventions. **Third**, the bare statement “a human being's essence is the same as its essence and quiddity” has no informative content, much less something requiring lengthy demonstration.

A more satisfactory explanation follows. The proofs that existence is *additional* to a thing establish only that what is **understood** by its existence is not what is understood by the thing itself. They do not establish that existence is a distinct accident inhering in it like an accident in a subject; the intellect rejects such a conclusion even where expressions in the Imām and others suggest it. Conversely, the proofs that existence is identical with a thing's essence establish only that the thing does not have one distinct external identity while an accident called its existence possesses a second distinct identity residing in the first, as whiteness resides in a body. They do not establish that what is **understood** by a thing's existence is exactly what is understood by that thing, a claim whose falsity is self-evident. Thus no genuine and tenable disagreement emerges between the parties about existence's being additional to quiddity **in the intellect**—that is, in conception and meaning. The intellect may attend to existence without quiddity or to quiddity without existence. It is not additional **in external identity**, as though each had an independent individual reality and one were an accident of the other like bodily whiteness. Once the question is properly specified, the dispute disappears. Equally, to say that *existence* is shared merely verbally, so that the existence attributed to a human and that attributed to a horse have utterly different meanings and share nothing in the concept of being, is an evasion of what is intellectually evident.

The author of *al-Mawāqif* relates this dispute to that over mental existence. Those who affirm mental existence assert that existence is additional in the intellect, in the sense that the intellect contains one item called existence and another called quiddity. Those who deny mental existence say simply that existence is identical with quiddity, since the two have no distinct identities outside the mind, and, on their view, there is no domain beyond the external one in which one could obtain without the other and thereby become distinct. There is a difficulty here. Those denying mental existence do not deny that we understand universals, considerational objects, nonexistents, and impossibles, or that these are conceptually distinct. They dispute only whether the process of understanding consists in something's occurring within the intellect and whether this requires a form of establishment. Denying mental existence therefore does not by itself justify denying **conceptual** diversity between existence and quiddity, or the meaningful commonness of existence, any more than it eliminates the difference between the concept of a human and a horse, or of possibility and impossibility, or the common application of each to its instances. At most such thinkers should decline to say that existence is an **extra item established in the mind** and that the common universal is **established there**. They can still say that existence is additional and shared *intellectually*, in intellection: the mind understands something different by one concept and the other, and apprehends a single universal meaning predicable of all the relevant instances. Accordingly the majority even among those who deny mental existence agree that existence is common in meaning and conceptually additional to quiddity, in the sense just explained.

title: The Necessary Existent: particular existence and its conceptual concomitant
en:
**On the words, “This is so in the case of the possible.”** What has been said about the absence of a genuine dispute—existence being additional to quiddity in the intellect because the concepts differ, yet identical in external reality because there are not two externally distinct individual identities—concerns possible things. In the case of the Necessary, the theologians affirm a reality beyond the intellect's grasp which of itself requires its own particular existence. This existence differs from that reality in concept, not in external identity, as with possible things. The philosophers, by contrast, hold that the Necessary's very reality is a particular, self-subsistent existence, both intellectually and externally. It requires neither a producing agent nor a subject in which to subsist, even in the intellect, and differs in reality from the existence of possible beings, while sharing with them the property of falling under unrestricted existence. They call this “pure existence” or “existence under the condition of not,” meaning that it does not subsist in a quiddity, even intellectually, as the existences of possibles do.

Their reason is that if the Necessary had both quiddity and existence, either the Necessary would be their combination—involving composition even in the intellect—or would be one of the two, involving dependence: quiddity would need existence in order to obtain, while existence, insofar as it inheres, would need quiddity even intellectually. **Objection:** The particular existence must itself depend on unrestricted existence, since what is particular cannot obtain without what is general. **Reply:** It is a particular being that obtains by itself, not through an agent; stands by itself, not through a quiddity; and requires neither unrestricted existence nor any other accidents or causes for its obtaining. It differs from other existences in reality, although unrestricted existence is truly predicated of it as an extrinsic, nonconstitutive concomitant. That common predicate neither compounds it nor makes it dependent. The same theologian who calls the Necessary a quiddity which exists does not suppose that its being narrower than unrestricted *quiddity* and *existent* makes it dependent upon those general concepts. How could it, when a general or unrestricted concept is purely considerational?

**Further objection:** Why could this reality, self-subsisting, independent of every other, and different from other realities, not be something *other than existence*? **Reply:** What obtains through itself, needing nothing else, cannot be something other than existence, for it is necessary that what is *not itself existence* needs existence in order to obtain. **Further objection:** Existence is one concept, and becomes many particular shares only through relation to different quiddities, like the whiteness of this snow and that snow; the restricted concept is just the unrestricted one plus a qualifying relation. **Reply:** Particular existences are distinct shares and multiple realities through themselves, not merely through the addition of a relative accident, which would make them identical in reality, or through specific differentiae, which would make unrestricted existence their genus. Unrestricted existence is their necessary concomitant, just as the light of the sun and that of a lamp differ in reality and effects while sharing *light*; the whiteness of snow and ivory similarly share *whiteness*, quantity and quality share accidentality, and substance and accident share possibility and existence. The absence of distinct conventional names for each kind of existence, comparable to the names of kinds of possible substances and accidents, has encouraged the mistaken belief that different existences are only portions of one reality distinguished by their relation to their quiddities. Fairness requires saying that real difference between Necessary and possible existence is correct, that a similar difference between substance and accident or between enduring and non-enduring existence is possible, but that it is not correct to say this of, for example, the existences of a human and a horse or those of Zayd and ʿAmr.

title: The Imām's objection concerning two existences
en:
**On the words, “If you say.”** Al-Fārābī and Ibn Sīnā seem to state that the Necessary's reality is a particular existence of which unrestricted existence—the shared opposite of nonexistence—is predicated, as summarized by the critical philosopher. The Imām objects that this admits the Necessary's existence to be additional to His reality and makes Him an existent possessing *two* existences, with no reason for making one of them the accident rather than the subject. We have already noted that the dispute concerns particular existences, not the unrestricted concept.

Some who sought to state the philosophers' view more precisely therefore said that a *share of the concept of being in concrete reality* is additional to the separate existence that is the principle of possible beings and is identical with the Necessary's essence. This seems to strengthen the objection: the share of being would be additional to the Necessary's reality as in possible things, giving the Necessary one existence as subject and another as accident. In a possible thing, such as a human, the account would imply three items: a quiddity, rational animal; an existence, its share in the concept of being; and a third thing, the particular reality which falls under the predicate *existence*, inheres in quiddity, and is itself the subject of that share. No one has proposed or proved such an analysis. Applied to the whiteness of snow, it would similarly posit one whiteness as a share in the universal concept and another particular whiteness which both inheres in snow and serves as the subject of that share.

The reply is that a *share of the concept of being* is simply the concept with some particular qualification, not an additional, particular ontological item identical with what the universal concept is predicated of. There is no dispute that the concept of being, and equally the concept considered with a qualification, differs from the Necessary's unknowable reality. Indeed all agree that the Necessary's reality is not known, whereas being is known—even self-evident—and the qualification of necessity is also known. The dispute is whether His **particular existence** has a quiddity conceptually distinct from it, as happens with possible things. Once a share of the universal concept is understood as the concept with an added qualification, everyone who holds that the universal is predicated by gradation, and that such a predicate must be a nonconstitutive accident of its instances rather than their essence or an essential part, has thereby distinguished in possible beings the quiddity, the common concept or share in being, and the particular existence through which the possible thing is externally actual—or rather which is that very actuality. Any demonstration establishing the former distinction establishes the latter, but the difference is **intellectual**, not an additional thing in external reality. A human being does not possess one independently distinct external thing called quiddity and another called existence, much less two distinct existences. Even if we supposed existence added to quiddity externally like snow's whiteness, the universal concept or its share would still be a merely intellectual representation. Moreover, subject and predicate have to be externally identical when one is truthfully predicated of the other. Neither two external existences in a human nor two whitenesses in snow follow.

title: The claim that the Necessary is unrestricted existence itself
en:
**On the words, “Then a group.”** A view has become widespread among some philosophers and Sufis that the Necessary's reality is **unrestricted existence itself**. They argue that the Necessary cannot be nonexistence or nonexistent, plainly; nor a quiddity existing, or a quiddity conjoined with existence, which would involve need and composition. He must therefore be existence. Nor can He be particular existence: if the particular is taken together with the unrestricted concept it is composite, and if taken as a share that is a subject of the universal, it depends upon what is unrestricted. Were unrestricted existence eliminated, they argue, every existence would be eliminated.

When objected that unrestricted existence is a **universal concept** which has no external realization in its own right, has countless instances, and cannot be the one unmultiplied Necessary, they say that it is one individual externally existing through an existence that is itself. Only the *existents* multiply, by its relative connections: relating that one existence to a human makes a human existent, to a horse makes a horse existent, and so forth. Accordingly, they interpret “the Necessary is existent” to mean that His essence is existence, whereas “a human is existent” or “a horse is existent” means that the thing possesses existence through a relation to the Necessary. Al-Taftāzānī regards this as a way of avoiding the scandal of directly saying that the Necessary is not an existent, or that every existence, including what belongs to impure or base things, is necessary; he rejects these implications emphatically.

His first reply is that existence's having many instances, and unrestricted existence's being a universal concept realized only in the intellect, are intellectually evident. The assumption that the particular needs the universal has the order backward: it is the universal that obtains only within the particular. A universal that forms an **essential constituent** of the particular is necessary for understanding it; a universal that is merely an **accidental predicate** is not needed in that way. Nor does the claim “if unrestricted existence vanished, all existence including the Necessary would vanish” prove the unrestricted universal necessary. Necessity would follow only if it were impossible for unrestricted existence to be absent **through its own essence**. It could instead be impossible for the universal to be eliminated entirely because that would entail the elimination of one of its instances, the Necessary—just as the concomitants of the Necessary, including quiddity, causality, and receptivity, cannot all be eliminated if the Necessary exists. **Objection:** Existence is necessarily non-nonexistent through itself, since a thing cannot possess its own contradictory. **Reply:** A contradiction occurs if we predicate “nonexistence” *directly* of existence, as in “existence is nonexistence.” It does not follow from the derived predicate “existence is not an existent.” Philosophers themselves agree that unrestricted existence is one of the **second intelligibles** and a considerational object without an independent external occurrence.

Supporters of the identity of the Necessary with unrestricted existence appeal to passages in philosophical writings. **First**, philosophers call the Necessary *pure existence* and *existence without qualification*. But these expressions need not denote the completely unrestricted universal. **Second**, they say existence is pure good: evil as such is the nonexistence of a thing or of a fitting perfection, and although existence may lead to the absence of something's perfection and thus be bad *relative to it*, evil here arises through that privation, not from existence itself. Where privation is wholly absent, so is evil. **Third**, they say existence has no opposite and no likeness. In the common account, an opposite is an existent equally strong as another and opposed to it; even if existence is called an existent in the sense of being the subject of the predicate existence, no existent can oppose existence itself. In the more specialized account, opposites share a subject while being incapable of simultaneous inherence; a subject is supposed to have independent subsistence from the qualities in it, which no subject can have in relation to existence. Even granting that point, there cannot be two existences replacing one another in the same subject as opposites. **Fourth**, they say existence has no genus or differentia. It is simple, not composite externally or intellectually; otherwise its parts would have to precede it in existence, externally or mentally as appropriate, so existence would precede itself. If the putative part were existent or existence it would already presuppose what it helps compose; if nonexistent or nonexistence the whole would be preceded by its contradictory. No genus could be wider than existence, since every thing belongs under existence. Some premises in these arguments are weak, but even if conceded they establish only that **both existence and the Necessary** have the cited features. Two affirmative propositions of that form yield no conclusion in the second syllogistic figure. The possession of properties also shared by the Necessary does not make unrestricted existence the Necessary unless the properties are proved **coextensive** with what is necessary.

The view also directly contradicts assertions made by its alleged philosophical authorities. They call unrestricted existence an **intellectual predicate**: something which cannot subsist without an intellectual subject and cannot have extramental inherence in it, such as possibility and quiddity. This differs from a human, which subsists independently of a subject, and from whiteness, which subsists in an external subject. They also classify unrestricted existence as a **second intelligible**: an intellectual attribute attaching to first intelligibles without something externally corresponding to that attribute, like universality, particularity, essentiality, and accidentality. These are features of realities as apprehended in the intellect; externally there is a human or blackness, not an additional entity called universality or essentiality. There is a qualification to be examined: this explanation seems to characterize the existences of things as intellectual predicates and second intelligibles, whereas the dispute concerns **unrestricted existence**. Their authorities also divide existence into necessary and possible, and into eternal and originated. The latter division depends on being or not being preceded by another or by nonexistence, the former on requiring or not requiring a cause. They hold that existence multiplies with its particular subjects—Zayd and ʿAmr as individuals, human and horse as species, animal and plant as genera. In this discussion *subject* means the thing of which the derived predicate *existent* is true, not an independently subsisting substrate of an externally inhering accident. Even if the language of inherence is retained, here the inherence is intellectual, since quiddity can be considered apart from existence, although it is never completely separated from intellectual existence.

These formulations might suggest that possible existences are nothing more than unrestricted existence multiplied by its relations to receptive quiddities, rather than independently diverse realities of which unrestricted existence is predicated. A more careful formulation would say that unrestricted existence has multiple **particular instances** as its subjects multiply. The philosophers also say that existence is predicated of the different existences **by gradation**. All these features are impossible as descriptions of the exalted Necessary itself. In brief, making the Necessary identical with unrestricted existence rests on false principles—for example, treating a universal as one individual externally existent, intrinsically incapable of nonexistence—and destroys accepted principles, such as that existence is the best-known concept, shared by different existences, predicated of them by gradation and numbered among second intelligibles. It would also undermine that the Necessary is the cause of the existences of possible things and is characterized by knowledge, power, will, life, sending messengers, revealing scriptures, and other matters made known by revelation. This last series records al-Taftāzānī's polemical consequences, not a neutral description of every philosopher or Sufi who uses the expression *absolute existence*.

First, philosophers call the Necessary pure existence and existence without qualification. But these expressions need not denote the completely unrestricted universal. Second, they say existence is pure good: evil as such is the nonexistence of a thing or of a fitting perfection, and although existence may lead to the absence of something's perfection and thus be bad relative to it, evil here arises through that privation, not from existence itself. Where privation is wholly absent, so is evil. Third, they say existence has no opposite and no likeness. In the common account, an opposite is an existent equally strong as another and opposed to it; even if existence is called an existent in the sense of being the subject of the predicate existence, no existent can oppose existence itself. In the more specialized account, opposites share a subject while being incapable of simultaneous inherence; a subject is supposed to have independent subsistence from the qualities in it, which no subject can have in relation to existence. Even granting that point, there cannot be two existences replacing one another in the same subject as opposites. Fourth, they say existence has no genus or differentia. It is simple, not composite externally or intellectually; otherwise its parts would have to precede it in existence, externally or mentally as appropriate, so existence would precede itself. If the putative part were existent or existence it would already presuppose what it helps compose; if nonexistent or nonexistence the whole would be preceded by its contradictory. No genus could be wider than existence, since every thing belongs under existence. Some premises in these arguments are weak, but even if conceded they establish only that both existence and the Necessary have the cited features. Two affirmative propositions of that form yield no conclusion in the second syllogistic figure. The possession of properties also shared by the Necessary does not make unrestricted existence the Necessary unless the properties are proved coextensive with what is necessary.

The view also directly contradicts assertions made by its alleged philosophical authorities. They call unrestricted existence an intellectual predicate: something which cannot subsist without an intellectual subject and cannot have extramental inherence in it, such as possibility and quiddity. This differs from a human, which subsists independently of a subject, and from whiteness, which subsists in an external subject. They also classify unrestricted existence as a second intelligible: an intellectual attribute attaching to first intelligibles without something externally corresponding to that attribute, like universality, particularity, essentiality, and accidentality. These are features of realities as apprehended in the intellect; externally there is a human or blackness, not an additional entity called universality or essentiality. There is a qualification to be examined: this explanation seems to characterize the existences of things as intellectual predicates and second intelligibles, whereas the dispute concerns unrestricted existence. Their authorities also divide existence into necessary and possible, and into eternal and originated. The latter division depends on being or not being preceded by another or by nonexistence, the former on requiring or not requiring a cause. They hold that existence multiplies with its particular subjects—Zayd and ʿAmr as individuals, human and horse as species, animal and plant as genera. In this discussion subject means the thing of which the derived predicate existent is true, not an independently subsisting substrate of an externally inhering accident. Even if the language of inherence is retained, here the inherence is intellectual, since quiddity can be considered apart from existence, although it is never completely separated from intellectual existence.

These formulations might suggest that possible existences are nothing more than unrestricted existence multiplied by its relations to receptive quiddities, rather than independently diverse realities of which unrestricted existence is predicated. A more careful formulation would say that unrestricted existence has multiple particular instances as its subjects multiply. The philosophers also say that existence is predicated of the different existences by gradation. All these features are impossible as descriptions of the exalted Necessary itself. In brief, making the Necessary identical with unrestricted existence rests on false principles—for example, treating a universal as one individual externally existent, intrinsically incapable of nonexistence—and destroys accepted principles, such as that existence is the best-known concept, shared by different existences, predicated of them by gradation and numbered among second intelligibles. It would also undermine that the Necessary is the cause of the existences of possible things and is characterized by knowledge, power, will, life, sending messengers, revealing scriptures, and other matters made known by revelation. This last series records al-Taftāzānī's polemical consequences, not a neutral description of every philosopher or Sufi who uses the expression absolute existence.

title: A catalogue of disputes over the nature of existence
en: **On the words, “How astonishing is the condition of existence!”** The author expresses surprise at how deeply intellectual authorities dispute existence's attributes while agreeing that it is better known than anything else. Normally a thing's attributes follow its essence in being clear or obscure. The disputed questions include: **(1) Is existence particular or universal?** Some call it one true individual with no multiplicity at all, treating the variety of existents as products of relational attribution, so “Zayd's existence” and “ʿAmr's existence” would resemble “Zayd's God” and “ʿAmr's God.” The correct answer is that existence is a universal with individual instances. **(2) Is it necessary or possible?** Many later writers call it necessary, on the understanding just refuted, which al-Taftāzānī characterizes as a grave error. **(3) Is it accident, substance, or neither?** The correct position is neither, since substance and accident are divisions of possible being. The Imām's language sometimes suggests it is an accident, and many theologians assert this, but the claim is extremely remote: an accident needs a subject that can subsist without it, whereas nothing can subsist or obtain without existence. **(4) Is existence itself existent?** Some say it exists through an existence identical with it, avoiding regress. Others hold that unrestricted existence is purely considerational, without external occurrence. If it had its own added existence the series would regress; if its existence were simply itself the term *existent* would be predicated in different senses of existence and of other things—*existence* in the first case and *having existence* in the second. Moreover, if existence were substance it could not be a quality of things; if accident, its subject would subsist without it, impossible for existence. And just as we conceive quiddity yet doubt its existence, we can conceive existence and doubt the **existence of existence**: if the latter is real and additional, regress follows. This also challenges those philosophers who identify the Necessary's quiddity with separate existence, since after conceiving that separate existence we still seek a demonstration that it obtains externally. Its external existence would be additional, and regress threatens again. The only escape proposed here is to treat existence predicated of existences as an intellectual consideration. Yet another group makes existence neither existent nor nonexistent, a supposed intermediate state to be discussed below. **(5) Are particular existences identical with their quiddities or additional to them?** This has been discussed. **(6) Does the term *existence* signify distinct concepts as a homonym, a single concept equally predicated of its instances, or one concept predicated with gradation?** The third is correct: the one meaning of being is not applied with complete equality of priority, appropriateness, or intensity.
